27755:
Colossians 3:3–4 gives three compelling reasons for Christians to keep seeking the things above. First, believers have died with Christ: they are no longer condemned by God’s law, ruled by worldly passions, or defined by the ambitions of this world. Second, their true life is hidden with Christ in God. Though the world may misunderstand or despise them, Christ securely holds their eternal life and is himself their present source of nourishment, satisfaction and strength. Third, Christ will return in glory, and his people will be revealed with him.

These past, present and future realities call for an energetic pursuit of heaven rather than a reluctant or divided response. The sermon urges believers to refuse pleasures and ambitions that choke their usefulness to Christ, while recognising that ordinary work, homes and possessions are not wrong in themselves. Earthly gifts should serve heavenly purposes. Christians are encouraged to delight in Christ, teach their children about him, love and serve the church, spread the gospel and endure sacrifice with confidence. The message also pleads with unbelievers not to reject Christ’s gracious offer of forgiveness and eternal life, but to come to him while there is still opportunity.
27756:
Colossians 3:1–2 calls believers who have been raised with Christ to keep seeking the things above and to set their minds there. The sermon explains that Colossians moves from doctrine to daily conduct while remaining centred on the sufficiency of Jesus. Christians were once spiritually dead and enslaved to sin, but God raised them with Christ, gave them eternal life and freed them to follow their Lord. Seeking heaven is therefore not an optional extra. It is the fitting response of people whose life, identity and power now come from Christ.

This pursuit is active, continuous and directed toward Christ himself—his kingdom, purposes, values and pleasure. It does not require abandoning work or ordinary responsibilities. Instead, every decision, relationship and ambition is to be assessed from a heavenly perspective. Because the mind is the gateway to the affections, believers should deliberately fill it with God’s word, prayer, worship and fellowship rather than allowing money, criticism, entertainment or worldly anxiety to dominate their attention. When spiritual desire feels weak, the answer is not greater distraction but renewed meditation on Christ. The sermon urges wholehearted devotion: earthly gifts may be used wisely, but they must be placed at the service of the King rather than competing with him.
27763:
Philippians 4:4–5 commands believers to rejoice in the Lord always and to let their gentle spirit be known to everyone. This joy is not a passing mood produced by comfortable circumstances, possessions, relationships or successful ministry. Paul writes while confined and opposed, yet repeats the command because Christian joy is rooted in the unchanging person of Jesus Christ. The sermon describes joy as deep satisfaction in what the heart loves and urges believers to examine whether disappointment reveals that they have placed their hope in something other than the Lord.

Christians can rejoice through trials because Christ is near, salvation is secure, and the Holy Spirit’s joy is already present in them. They cultivate that joy by remembering God’s saving work, looking to Christ, praying, reading Scripture, worshipping, serving and trusting God’s providence. Rejoicing does not deny pain; it views every circumstance under God’s wise care and remembers that Christ will return. Joy then becomes visible as gentleness, patience, graciousness and peace toward both believers and unbelievers. The message calls the church to reject grumbling and harshness, encourage one another with joyful faith, and present the good news of Christ with a manner that matches its hope.
27765:
Colossians 2:20–23 warns Christians against legalism: relying on human rules, external practices and self-denial as though they could produce spiritual life or acceptance with God. Believers have died with Christ to the condemning principles of the world, so they must not return to bondage under decrees such as “do not handle, taste or touch.” God’s commands still matter, but Christian obedience flows from gratitude for Christ’s finished work rather than fear that keeping rules will earn righteousness. Legalism replaces this freedom with man-made standards and then imposes them on others.

The sermon identifies several fruits of that error. Legalism becomes judgmental because self-righteous people measure others by rules they can keep. It becomes negative because criticism helps them feel superior. It also concentrates on appearances while neglecting the heart, producing impressive-looking religion that cannot restrain sinful desires. The answer is not less obedience, but deeper reliance on Christ. He gives believers a new nature, his Spirit, his word and the fellowship of the church so that obedience can express love for him and cultivate godly desires. Christians are urged to search their hearts, abandon self-righteousness and rest in Christ alone, while unbelievers are called to surrender every claim of merit and run to him for cleansing.
27766:
Colossians 2:16–19 warns the church about two ways false teaching draws people away from the sufficiency of Christ. Legalism says that acceptance with God and spiritual growth depend on human achievement, religious rules or external observances. It judges Christians over food, festivals and other matters that are shadows rather than substance. Paul does not forbid choices in matters where Scripture is silent, but he refuses to let anyone bind another believer’s conscience. Christian freedom is not permission for self-centred living; choices should still be made according to whether they honour Christ and draw the believer nearer to him.

Mysticism substitutes private visions, spiritual experiences and impressive displays of humility for confidence in Christ and his word. Such claims can inflate people with pride, grant them false authority and place others under their control. Paul directs believers instead to hold fast to Christ, the head who supplies and grows his whole body. The sermon urges the church to test its own heart, reject both self-righteous effort and unverifiable spiritual claims, and cling to Jesus alone. He has forgiven sin, defeated the enemy and provides everything necessary for growth through his Spirit, his word and his care for the church. The path forward is faithful obedience flowing from completeness in Christ.
27767:
Colossians 2:11–15 explains what it means for believers to be complete in Christ amid a broken world that cannot satisfy the soul. The sermon traces three works Jesus has accomplished for his people. First, he performs the true circumcision of the heart: not an outward ritual, but God’s work of removing the old resistant nature and giving new desires that seek and love him. Through union with Christ in his death, burial and resurrection, believers have been brought from spiritual death into new life and freed from sin’s former mastery.

Second, Christ has forgiven all their transgressions. The condemning record of debt that stood against them was taken away and nailed to his cross, where he bore the penalty that belonged to them. Christians can therefore resist accusations that drive them from God and instead enjoy unhindered fellowship with him. Third, through his death and resurrection, Jesus disarmed the rulers and authorities and publicly triumphed over them. His victory means believers need not live as though the enemy still owns them. The message calls Christians to stop seeking fulfilment in creation or in anxious self-effort, rest in Christ’s complete work, repent when they sin, and delight confidently in God. Unbelievers are urged to confess their need and come to the Saviour who forgives sinners.
27780:
Paul’s appeal to Euodia and Syntyche in Philippians 4 shows why peace within the church matters. These women were genuine believers and active gospel workers, yet conflict had disrupted their harmony. Paul addresses both without taking sides and urges them to agree in the Lord. His loving directness shows that ignoring a quarrel is not kindness: unresolved strife can grow, draw others into opposing camps, and weaken the whole church. Christian unity is not built merely on shared interests or personalities, but on Christ, the gospel, and the heavenly hope believers hold together.

The sermon therefore calls Christians to address conflict promptly and humbly. Each person should seek reconciliation without hiding behind who started the dispute, remaining teachable when another believer offers help. Paul also calls a trusted companion to help the women, reminding the church that peacemaking is a shared responsibility carried out gently, without gossip or favouritism. Believers are encouraged to examine whether they solve problems or create them, to receive wise help when needed, and to remember the grace Christ has shown them. Those who are not reconciled to God are urged first to turn to Jesus in repentance and faith. The church honours Christ as its members pursue peace, bear one another’s burdens, and keep striving together for the gospel.
27781:
Colossians 2:8–10 warns believers not to be captured by philosophy and empty deception that arise from human tradition rather than Christ. The sermon places this warning within Paul’s response to teaching that undermined both the sufficiency of Christ and the authority of God’s word. Human wisdom is not condemned simply because it involves thought or learning; the danger is pursuing an account of life, morality, guilt, or God that refuses to submit to Jesus. Such ideas may appear clever and persuasive, yet they cannot overcome humanity’s deepest problem or bring people into a true knowledge of God. Christians are therefore called to remain alert, test teaching carefully, and refuse to treat discernment as unloving judgment.

Paul’s answer is the fullness of Christ. In Jesus, the fullness of deity dwells bodily, and believers have been made complete in him. Christ is neither one spiritual power among many nor merely a guide toward God: he is presented as truly God and truly human, ruling over every authority. The sermon urges listeners to bring their reasoning under Christ, seek answers in Scripture, and rest in his saving work rather than chasing fulfilment through worldly systems. A life filled with Christ learns to face guilt, purpose, obedience, and hope through him, following him with humility and confidence.
27783:
Paul’s appeal to “stand firm in the Lord” is surrounded by warm affection for the Philippian church. Before giving the command, he calls them his beloved brethren, says he longs to see them, and names them his joy and crown. The sermon presents this as a model of compassionate Christian encouragement. Paul does not motivate people through threats, irritation, or self-importance. Though he is an apostle, he approaches them first as a humble brother whose unconditional love reflects the Father’s love for the Son and Christ’s love for his church. His desire is not distant goodwill but fellowship and their growth toward the heavenly city.

This affection gives strength to the command. Standing firm is a continuing, active responsibility for every believer, like soldiers holding their position together under attack. Yet it can be done only “in the Lord,” abiding in Christ and relying on the strength he supplies. The church protects and encourages one another when its members value fellow believers above status, comfort, possessions, or achievement. The sermon asks what believers count as their joy and crown, whether they long for fellowship, and how they serve the local body in deeds as well as words. Against a self-centred culture, Christians are called to love patiently, humbly, and sacrificially so they can run together for the gospel.
27929:
Colossians 2:4–7 equips believers to resist persuasive teaching that draws them away from Christ. Paul points first to Jesus, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are found, and then gives practical encouragement for remaining steady. Christians are to stand together like disciplined soldiers, protecting one another and holding their ground through a settled faith in Christ. They are also to continue walking in the same Christ Jesus they received—not merely accepting facts about him, but trusting him as Messiah, Saviour, and Lord and gladly placing every part of life under his rule.

The sermon develops Paul’s images into five memorable responses: be a good soldier, a faithful follower, a healthy tree, a diligent student, and a grateful worshipper. Believers grow by being rooted and built up in Christ, drawing their spiritual nourishment and identity from him rather than from possessions, comfort, or approval. They strengthen their understanding through careful study of Scripture so that they can recognise error instead of following an imagined Jesus. Yet knowledge must reach the heart. Gratitude for Christ’s saving work produces joy and contentment, weakening the appeal of teaching that promises something better than him. The message calls Christians to cling to Christ together, learn his word deeply, and let thankful worship overflow from a life satisfied in him.
27933:
Colossians 2:3–4 declares that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ. The sermon presents Jesus as God’s inexhaustible gift: believers not only receive him, but discover greatness they can never exhaust. Christ is the source and embodiment of wisdom, sovereignly giving understanding and never needing counsel himself. Paul’s word “treasures” directs attention especially to the priceless knowledge of God and salvation. Forgiveness, spiritual growth, hope, and a true knowledge of the Father are not found through secret experiences or persuasive alternatives, but through Jesus alone. This truth protects the church from teaching that sounds clever while moving people away from him.

Knowing Christ also reveals the character of God clearly. At the cross, the sermon explains, God’s justice against sin and his mercy toward sinners meet; his hatred of sin and his extraordinary love are displayed in the suffering and saving work of his Son. This gives believers confidence when life is confusing: they may not know what the future holds, but Christ does, and he is able to guide them. The message therefore calls listeners to make knowing Jesus their great pursuit, replacing distraction and spiritual laziness with attentive study, trust, and worship. Those who remain outside Christ are urged to come to him for salvation rather than merely knowing facts about him.
27934:
In Colossians 2:1–2, Paul reveals his struggle for believers he has never met. Though imprisoned and unable to visit them, he labours through writing and prayer because false teaching threatens to draw them away from the all-sufficient Christ. His concern is more than a feeling: it is work for their spiritual strength. Paul models a love that refuses self-pity and finds a way to serve. The sermon invites Christians to share this active concern, praying for believers, grieving when they are deceived, and working for their good when distance or weakness limits what they can do.

Paul prays that their hearts will be strengthened as they are knit together in love. Knowing Jesus, the sermon explains, is a community project. Believers become like interwoven threads whose life forms a strong fabric. This love involves bearing burdens, offering hospitality, forgiving offences, meeting needs, and serving people beyond one’s comfort zone. As Christians embody Christ’s humility, gentleness, and care toward one another, they help each other see clearly that Jesus is sufficient. Their love produces deeper assurance, an intimate knowledge of Christ, and the wealth of being satisfied in him. The message therefore calls the church to resist isolated Christianity and make love a commitment, trusting that Christ makes himself known as his people care for one another.
27935:
Colossians 1:28–29 joins the church’s purpose to the power that makes it possible. Because Christ lives in his people as their hope of glory, they proclaim him—rather than themselves, human achievement, or a moral system. Their goal is to present every person mature in Christ, with thoughts, desires, and actions increasingly shaped by him. The sermon insists that this calling belongs to every believer. Different Christians may teach, pray, encourage, serve, or work behind the scenes, but no follower of Jesus is spiritually unemployed. As believers share their joy in Christ, that joy grows and they long for others to know and cherish him too.

This purpose involves real labour. Paul describes work carried to exhaustion and striving like an athlete pressing toward the finish, and his own life included hardship, rejection, danger, and deep concern for the churches. Yet endurance does not arise from natural toughness. Paul labours according to Christ’s power working mightily within him. The same indwelling Christ assures believers that they are known, accompanied, possessed, and ruled by their Lord. The sermon calls Christians to enjoy Christ’s presence, obey his commands, and place their lives at his disposal. Rather than retreating into comfort or self-pity, they can serve through weakness, trusting God’s power to sustain faithful proclamation and sacrificial care for others.
27937:
Isaiah 6:1–4 gives the church a vision of the Lord whose greatness can sustain unity among people of many backgrounds. In a year marked by a king’s death, moral decline, and national danger, Isaiah sees the King still seated on his throne. He is high and exalted, his majesty fills the temple, and no earthly change unsettles his reign. The sermon identifies this glorious Lord with Christ and urges believers to place circumstances—including trials, rulers, and uncertain futures—beneath his sovereign authority. A high view of God reshapes worship and life, drawing the church together around one supreme purpose rather than leaving fellowship as a brief weekly gathering.

The seraphim cry, “Holy, holy, holy,” declaring that God is unique and incomparable. His holiness is displayed in every attribute: he defines righteousness, possesses unmatched power, creates and sustains all things, and fills the earth with his glory. Even sinless angels cover themselves before him, yet they remain ready to serve and praise with wholehearted joy. Their worship teaches believers reverence, humility, readiness, and delight. The message calls the church to behold God as he truly is, proclaim his greatness, and put its hands together in service. As people share this vision of the holy and sovereign Lord, they find a foundation for loving unity, courageous prayer, and worship.
27938:
Colossians 1:28 captures the church’s great purpose in three words: “We proclaim him.” Because Christ lives in his people as their hope of glory, he becomes the centre of their message and life. Christians do not primarily announce themselves, personal achievements, moral techniques, or a religious system; they make Jesus known. The sermon traces this focus through Scripture and presents Christ as the fulfilment of God’s saving promises, the one in whom salvation and hope are found. Whether parents guide children, believers encourage one another, or the church speaks to unbelievers, every truth should lead attention toward Christ rather than away from him.

Paul describes two means of proclaiming Christ: admonishing and teaching every person with wisdom. Admonition lovingly corrects error, rebukes sin, and warns of danger; it is a responsibility shared by believers, not only leaders. Teaching explains the truth that gives such correction its meaning. Joined together, they connect right conduct with Christ as its motive, pattern, and goal, preventing correction from becoming a cold burden. The sermon encourages Christians to speak of Jesus in fellowship and apply his character to life’s challenges. It highlights his deity, majesty, humility, compassion, and grace, especially his willingness to suffer for sinners. The church therefore proclaims the whole Christ, seeking mature lives shaped by worship rather than mere outward conformity.
27939:
Colossians 1:26–27 unveils a mystery hidden through past ages but now made known to all God’s people: Christ in you, the hope of glory. This mystery is not a puzzle discovered by intelligence or reserved for an elite. God chose to reveal it by grace to saints, including Gentile believers outside Israel’s privileges. The astonishing truth is not merely that Christ gives blessings, stands beside his people, or thinks about them. The glorious Christ himself makes his home in them. The Creator dwells within his creatures, the sinless one within people struggling with sin, making this revelation humbling and wonderful.

The mystery is rich because the all-sufficient Christ is not distant. Believers possess him securely, may enjoy his presence, and are themselves possessed and ruled by him. He comforts, cleanses, strengthens, reshapes priorities, and creates a desire to obey from the heart. His indwelling power enables holiness and endurance through trials. Christ in his people is also their hope of glory—a confident expectation that he will carry them into resurrection life, fellowship, and the new creation. The sermon calls Christians to stop envying worldly advantages and instead seek a deeper experience of belonging to Jesus. Those outside Christ are invited to call on him for mercy, forgiveness, and the new life of his presence within.
27940:
Concluding a series on the attributes of God, this sermon from Exodus 34:14, "the Lord, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God", presents divine jealousy as the motivation believers need to resist the pull of a prosperous, distracting world. Unlike sinful jealousy, rooted in self and insecurity, God's jealousy is a holy zeal to protect what is rightly his and to keep an exclusive relationship, a consuming fire against all who dishonour him. First, God is jealous for his own glory. Creation, the image of God in humanity and redemption itself exist for his praise, and the first commandments forbid every rival god because he is jealous.

Second, God is jealous for his Son. The Father's zeal will establish Christ's endless kingdom and has placed all things under his feet, which is why salvation is found in no other name: Jesus alone will be honoured forever as Redeemer. Third, God is jealous for his people, as a faithful husband for his bride. His jealousy is loving, faithful in protecting his elect and holy in giving himself wholly to them, so he rightly calls for undivided devotion and grieves when they seek satisfaction in broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2). Believers are urged to confess their idols, thank Christ for bearing their unfaithfulness, follow him wholeheartedly, and ask not only whether something is sinful but whether it increases their delight in God.
27941:
Closing a series on the growing Christian, this sermon on Philippians 3:20-21 asks what drives believers to live faithfully in a world full of trials, temptation and sorrow, and answers with the Christian hope. First, the position of that hope: our citizenship is in heaven. Unlike the enemies of the cross who live for this world, believers are pilgrims bound for a better country prepared by God. Christians are urged not to be attached to or attracted by the world, despite pressure even from professing believers. Their citizenship can never be revoked by sickness, sorrow or sin, so they should store up treasure in heaven.

Second, the person of that hope: we eagerly wait for a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ. He came first as a humble servant but will return as a glorious King to consummate his marriage with his bride. Believers should long for him as a child waits for a parent or a bride for her groom, rather than for possessions, while unbelievers will dread his coming as Judge. Third, the possession of that hope: a new body. Christ will transform our weak, decaying bodies to be like his glorious body by the same power with which he subjects all things to himself, so we can stand in God's presence (1 Corinthians 15). Listeners are asked to examine their relationship with Christ and bear good fruit.
28074:
God’s mercy is presented as his compassionate response to sinful, hurting people. The sermon begins with the mercy seat in Israel’s sanctuary, showing that guilty people approach the holy Judge by relying on mercy rather than merit. God displays a general mercy toward all creation: he patiently withholds deserved judgment, provides life and goodness, and calls people to repent. Scripture’s story shows this patience, from the years before the flood to Jesus grieving over Jerusalem and praying for those who crucified him. Yet this patience must not be mistaken for permission to continue in sin, because the opportunity to receive mercy in this life will not last forever.

The sermon then describes God’s saving mercy toward those who come to Christ. It is sovereign, undeserved, abundant, tender, and everlasting. God saves not because he discovers righteousness in a person, but because his heart is merciful. Paul’s conversion illustrates compassion reaching a violent persecutor, while the father welcoming the prodigal son portrays God’s readiness to receive his returning children. Even loving discipline serves restoration rather than rejection. Because God’s mercy is greater than human sin, believers can return to him honestly instead of hiding in shame. The message invites every listener to abandon self-reliance, trust Jesus, and ask God for the forgiveness and cleansing that flow from his inexhaustible mercy.
28075:
The wrath of God is not an embarrassing truth to hide, but part of Scripture’s revelation of his holy character. The sermon explains that divine wrath is unlike a sinful human outburst or loss of temper. It is God’s settled, righteous opposition to evil and his just determination to judge it. Because God is a perfectly righteous Judge, indifference toward wickedness would deny his moral purity. Understanding his wrath also deepens an understanding of grace: the saving love of Christ shines more clearly when people recognise the judgment sinners deserve and the cost Jesus bore for them.

The message describes God’s wrath as fierce, pitiless, and terrifying, then surveys its expressions in history, at the end of the age, in the present condition of unbelief, in God’s judicial abandonment of persistent rebellion, and in final judgment. These warnings are intended to awaken sober attention rather than speculation. Today is presented as a day of mercy, when the call to repent can still be heard. The sermon urges listeners not to presume upon more time or plan to turn to God later. Christ is proclaimed as the sinless Saviour who bore wrath at the cross and rose again. Every listener is called to lay down self-righteousness, acknowledge sin honestly, and flee to Jesus for mercy, forgiveness, and life.
28076:
God’s transcendence and immanence belong together, giving a view of the God Scripture reveals. Transcendence means that God is infinitely exalted above and distinct from creation. He is not part of the universe or dependent upon it, but its Creator, sovereign Ruler, and sustaining Lord. His majesty does not fade like human greatness, and his thoughts encompass what people cannot see. This truth calls for reverence, frees believers from the fear of people, and encourages trust when God’s purposes are difficult to understand. His ways remain perfect even when the future is hidden from us.

Immanence means that this exalted God is also present and active within his world. His power governs creation, his authority extends everywhere, and his knowledge reaches every visible action and hidden thought. Yet God draws especially near to his people. The Son became human as Emmanuel, suffered, died, and rose so that those he saves could enjoy fellowship with him. By his Spirit, God dwells in believers and meets them with love, peace, joy, strength, and companionship. The sermon urges Christians facing guilt, loneliness, or heavy trials to remember that the sovereign God has not abandoned them. Because he is both above all things and lovingly near, they can bring anxieties to him, rest in his care, and approach his throne of grace through Christ.
28077:
Christian liberty is not permission to define good for ourselves or simply to escape every restraint. The sermon begins with Psalm 119:44–45, where the psalmist connects walking in liberty with seeking and keeping God’s precepts. Human beings make real choices, yet our motives are affected by sin; apart from Christ, even apparent freedom remains bondage. Christ frees his people from slavery to sin and makes them servants of righteousness. This is liberty within his loving rule: not doing whatever we please, but becoming able and willing to do what we ought.

The message describes this freedom through safety, provision, peace, a new nature, and loving obedience. Under Christ’s rule, believers find refuge, guidance through God’s word, peace from guilt through the cross, and a renewed desire to pursue righteousness. Christian liberty therefore grows as believers seek God’s commands, use the ordinary means of grace, and help one another endure seasons of trial. The sermon calls listeners to examine what motivates their obedience, to preach the gospel to themselves and one another, and to keep their eyes fixed on Jesus. Those who feel weary are invited to come to Christ, whose rule gives true rest rather than another form of captivity.
28078:
Philippians 3:18–19 follows Paul’s call to imitate godly examples with a serious warning about ungodly influence. Some people may speak like Christians and participate in a local church while their settled way of life denies the cross they profess. Paul warns the Philippians repeatedly and with tears because such people face destruction and can draw believers away from faithful pursuit of Christ. The sermon distinguishes avoiding their influence from abandoning evangelism: Christians should seek to lead unbelievers and false professors to Christ, but must not let them shape their doctrine, desires, or conduct.

Paul identifies these enemies of the cross by what rules their lives. Their appetites function as their god, they boast in what should bring shame, and their minds remain fixed on earthly things. These marks concern the direction of a life, not isolated possessions or ordinary responsibilities. In contrast, believers are to fill their minds with Christ, follow examples that display godliness, and continue toward their heavenly home. The warning should produce vigilance without pride, honest self-examination, and grief for people who remain outside Christ. Rather than being indifferent or easily influenced, the church is called to pray, speak the gospel, defend truth, pursue holiness, and help one another run faithfully toward Jesus.
28079:
In Colossians 1:24–25, Paul says that he rejoices in his sufferings for the church. This is not denial, forced optimism, or delight in pain. Paul knows grief and anguish, yet beneath them is a durable joy rooted beyond the rewards of this world. Imprisonment, rejection, physical hardship, and false accusation do not control him because his treasure, identity, and purpose are anchored in Christ and his coming kingdom. Suffering for Jesus also confirms that Paul belongs to the Master who was rejected before him, making hardship an honoured participation in Christ’s cause rather than evidence that God has forgotten him.

Paul’s afflictions do not add anything to Christ’s saving work. They accompany the spreading of that salvation through the preaching of the gospel. He endures them for Christ’s body, the church, loving both its Head and its members and standing for their freedom in Jesus. His willingness to suffer strengthens the credibility of the truth he teaches. Rejoicing in hardship also makes witness powerful: observers see a hope that loss cannot destroy. The sermon calls believers to serve the church without demanding repayment, continue speaking of Christ when rejected, and let suffering expose pride and deepen dependence on Jesus. As God meets them with grace, their joy can point others to the strength and worth of their Saviour.
28080:
Colossians 1:23 calls believers to continue in the faith, firmly established and unmoved from the hope of the gospel. The sermon presents this perseverance not as an uncertain condition by which genuine Christians keep earning salvation, but as the defining evidence of faith that God preserves. Those whose profession was never rooted in Christ may depart, while true believers continue clinging to him. Sanctification is therefore a journey in which Christians actively put sin to death and entrust every area of life to Jesus, yet their endurance rests upon God’s work rather than their strength alone.

Paul’s encouragement looks backward, at Christ’s completed work; around, at God’s present protection; and forward, to the hope secured in heaven. Jesus has redeemed, forgiven, reconciled, and accepted his people, and his love moves them to follow him with gratitude rather than fear. In the present, God preserves them by his power, the indwelling Holy Spirit, a renewed nature, his word, and even corrective discipline. Looking ahead, believers expect Christ to return, raise them, end their suffering, and bring them into fellowship and inheritance. This gospel hope helps them endure sacrifice without being captured by temporary rewards. The message calls Christians to keep trusting Christ, joyfully pursue holiness, and anchor their choices in what he has done, is doing, and will yet do.
28081:
Philippians 3:17 calls believers to join in following Paul’s example and to watch those who live according to the same pattern. Christian growth is not a solitary project. God brings his people into the church, where they receive encouragement, correction, practical wisdom, and living examples of faith. Mature believers are called to keep growing and pass what they learn to others, while others must seek models. Discipleship crosses age, ethnicity, personality, and shared interests because Christ binds the church together. Unembodied, unshared knowledge does not fulfil this calling.

Paul does not present himself as perfect or draw attention to his personality. He can say “follow me” because his life is being shaped by Christ. His pressing toward holiness, prayer, gratitude, concern for the church, endurance under hardship, gospel courage, humility, and joy provide patterns others can practise. Scripture similarly calls church leaders to be examples, but Paul also directs attention to other believers whose conduct reflects the same apostolic pattern. Each Christian remains responsible to observe, imitate, and grow; no mentor can obey on another person’s behalf. The sermon therefore asks whom we are following and whom we are influencing. Believers should seek people whose character displays Jesus, learn from them attentively, and become examples who help the next person pursue holiness and maturity in Christ.
28083:
Colossians 1:21–22 makes Christ’s work personal. Paul moves from Christ’s rule over all creation to the reconciliation of people who once lived as his enemies. The sermon first faces the bad news: apart from Jesus, humanity is alienated from God, hostile in mind, and engaged in evil deeds. Sin separates people from God’s presence, disorders their desires, and produces resistance to his rule. This account is not meant to glorify human failure, but to show the brightness of Christ’s grace. Minimising alienation also diminishes appreciation for the reconciliation Jesus accomplished.

The good news turns on Paul’s words, “yet he has now reconciled you.” While sinners were still hostile, Christ acted in love through the death of his body. Reconciliation removes enmity and restores peace with God, bringing believers into the fellowship for which forgiveness, redemption, and justification prepare the way. At the cross, Jesus bears sin, judgment, bondage, and guilt; by his work he also gives a new heart that finds God desirable. Paul says Christ will present his people holy, blameless, and beyond reproach—set apart for God, free from condemnation, and clothed in Christ’s righteousness. The sermon calls believers to treasure this peace through every trial, respond with gratitude, and surrender their lives to the Saviour whose mercy reached them when they were far away.
28084:
Colossians 1:19–20 gives two reasons for Christ’s preeminence: all fullness dwells in him, and all things are reconciled through him. The Father delights in his Son, and Jesus alone is sufficient to satisfy those who belong to him. Paul’s language answers teaching that divided divine fullness among spiritual intermediaries. God’s complete fullness—his power, wisdom, love, goodness, compassion, grace, and mercy—dwells personally in Christ. Nothing needed for salvation or spiritual life must be found in another mediator or religious technique. The sermon therefore urges listeners to look to Jesus rather than trusting the strength of their faith or repentance.

Through the blood of his cross, Christ also reconciles all things to himself. This does not mean every person or creature is saved. Sin has disordered creation, but Jesus’ death, resurrection, and exaltation place everything in its proper relationship beneath his authority. Evil spiritual powers are defeated and will face judgment; unbelieving people will answer to Christ as Judge; and those he redeems are brought into saving peace with him. All creation will finally acknowledge his lordship, willingly or unwillingly. This vision calls believers to give Jesus first place now. He is to direct their families, work, possessions, relationships, and decisions as the rightful King who conquered sin and death and rules over all things.
28085:
Colossians 1:18 presents Jesus Christ as the head of the body, the church, and calls believers to recognise his first place in everything. The sermon unfolds this picture through five aspects of Christ’s headship. He loves the church as his bride, shares with his people the blessings that belong to him, gives the church life, sustains its growth, and rules it as Lord. His people belong to him, yet he also gives himself to them with comfort, mercy, and strength. As every part of a body depends upon its head, the church receives life and direction from Christ. His resurrection as the firstborn from the dead confirms him as the living and reigning head who will never die again.

Christ supplies his church through the service of its members. Believers are therefore called to receive from him and use their gifts to build one another up in love, rather than blaming him for spiritual weakness while remaining inactive. Every ministry and gathering should be governed by Jesus and directed toward his honour. The sermon asks each listener to examine whether Christ has first place in relationships, work, worship, decisions, and desires. Because he is the loving Redeemer and supreme Lord, Christians can follow him willingly, treasure him above passing pleasures, and yield every area of life to his rule.
28086:
Colossians 1:16–17 exalts Jesus Christ as Creator, eternal Lord, and Sustainer of all things. Everything in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, came into being by him, through him, and for him. No angel or other creature assisted him, and every power remains beneath his authority. Creation therefore carries his ownership and exists for his glory. Jesus is also before all things. Unlike a world marked by beginnings, change, weakness, and decay, his character never changes. His enduring love, promises, and faithfulness give believers a secure foundation for trust.

The universe does not continue on its own after creation. Christ presently holds it together by his power, from its greatest structures to the smallest details of life. The One who died for sinners and rose again is also the One who sustains every breath. This truth offers hope to people burdened by sin, fear, loss, or unresolved trouble. The Creator has power to give a new heart, forgive sin, and bring eternal life; the eternal Saviour remains faithful; and the Sustainer never abandons those who depend upon him. The sermon calls listeners to worship Jesus, seek him in their need, and place his desires before their own. Because people were created for Christ, every part of life—including relationships, work, possessions, and speech—should honour him.
28087:
Psalm 73 traces Asaph’s movement from spiritual decline to renewed faith. He begins with the settled truth that God is good to his people, yet he nearly stumbles when he envies the apparent prosperity of the wicked. Looking only at what his eyes can see, he imagines that their wealth, ease, and pride make faithfulness pointless. His struggle grows into self-pity as he compares their comfort with his own discipline and suffering. The sermon warns that envy distorts perspective, tempts believers to doubt God’s goodness, and makes temporary pleasures seem more valuable than knowing Christ.

The turning point comes when Asaph enters God’s sanctuary. Worship, Scripture, and an eternal perspective reveal both the fragile end of worldly prosperity and the lasting security of God’s people. Asaph recognises his ignorance, but also sees that God has never released his hand: God guides him now and will receive him into glory. His complaint gives way to the confession that nothing in heaven or on earth compares with God, the strength of his heart and his portion forever. The sermon calls believers to draw near to God through worship, fellowship, prayer, and his Word. When envy or discouragement takes hold, they can confess it, remember God’s goodness, treasure Christ above the world, and tell others of his works.
28088:
Romans 12:2 explains how believers live out the dedication described in the previous verse. A once-for-all commitment to present the body to God is followed by two continuing commands: do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed through the renewing of the mind. The world presses people into its patterns, values, ambitions, and assumptions. Even activities that are not plainly sinful can weaken devotion when they feed materialism, sensuality, violence, wasted time, or the desire for approval. Christians are called to resist whatever shapes their lives contrary to the new heart God has given them.

Resistance alone is not enough. Lasting change comes as the Holy Spirit transforms believers while they deliberately fill their minds with the truth and glory of Christ in Scripture. This renewal changes desires, speech, choices, and character. It also enables Christians to experience God’s will as good, pleasing, and perfect rather than as a burden. The sermon describes people as pleasure seekers and urges them not merely to suppress worldly desires, but to seek satisfaction in Christ. Security is found in his faithful care, honour in exalting him, and justice in his righteous rule. By turning from the world and beholding Jesus, believers can remain devoted under pressure, obey from the heart, and follow Christ even when faithfulness is costly.
28089:
First Peter 1:3–5 calls suffering believers to praise the God of salvation. Peter directs their attention away from hardship and toward what God has done, what he has promised, and how he keeps his people. According to his great mercy, God causes sinners to be born again. The new birth is more than forgiveness: those who were spiritually dead receive life, new desires, the indwelling Spirit, adoption into God’s family, and the righteousness of Christ. This work begins with God’s grace and produces a response of faith, gratitude, obedience, and praise.

Through Christ’s resurrection, believers are born into a living hope. His rising confirms their present new life and their future resurrection, giving assurance rather than uncertain optimism. God also gives his children an inheritance that cannot perish, become defiled, or fade. It is kept in heaven by God, beyond every source of loss and corruption. At the same time, God’s power guards believers through faith until salvation is revealed. This security does not make faithful living unnecessary; it strengthens Christians to persevere, obey, and serve while trusting God’s care. The sermon invites listeners to remember the cost of the cross, praise God in both joy and suffering, live for his will rather than possessions, and come to Christ for the new birth they cannot produce for themselves.
28091:
Psalm 119:1–8 answers the search for lasting happiness by directing people to God, the source of blessing. The psalmist first looks at those whose lives are shaped by God’s Word. They walk in his ways, treasure his testimony, seek him wholeheartedly, and refuse to make peace with sin. This blamelessness is not sinless perfection. Believers fall, but they repent, rise again, and continue pursuing Christ because they find greater pleasure in him than in disobedience. True happiness therefore rests neither in money nor possessions, but in communion with God and a life ordered by his truth.

The psalmist then looks toward heaven and recognises that God has commanded his precepts to be kept diligently. Grace does not change what is holy; through Christ it changes the believer’s relationship to God’s law. Christ has borne condemnation and supplied righteousness, so the law becomes a friend and guide rather than a condemning master. Finally, the psalmist looks at himself and prays that his ways will be established. He longs for holiness, assurance, gratitude, and dependence upon grace. The sermon calls Christians to examine whether they are growing, confess wandering desires, seek God with their whole heart, and pray for strength to obey. Diligent walking fosters assurance, while reliance on God guards against self-confidence and keeps believers pressing toward him.
28093:
Romans 12:1 calls every Christian to complete devotion to God. Paul’s appeal rests on the mercies unfolded throughout Romans: justification, peace, reconciliation, grace, adoption, hope, resurrection, and the inseparable love of God in Christ. Believers do not offer themselves in order to earn mercy. Because God has already shown mercy through Jesus, gratitude becomes the motive for a wholehearted response. Healthy doctrine fuels godly living, and a clear view of the gospel moves Christians to place their lives at God’s disposal.

Paul describes this response as presenting the body as a living and holy sacrifice. The body is not evil, but it carries desires that resist holiness and must be brought under the Spirit’s rule. To present it is a decisive commitment, like an enduring vow; to be holy is to belong entirely to God without reserving cherished sins, relationships, plans, or pleasures; and to be living is to continue that dedication through ordinary life. Christian worship therefore extends beyond gathered meetings into work, rest, conversation, relationships, thoughts, and choices. The sermon does not promise sinless perfection, but calls believers to fight sin and embrace God’s commands for life. Such surrender is pleasing worship, frees Christians from being ruled by fear or worldly ambition, and prepares them to remain faithful when obedience becomes costly.
28094:
Colossians 1:13 gives believers a reason for gratitude: the Father has rescued them from the power of darkness and transferred them into the kingdom of his beloved Son. The sermon describes darkness as Satan’s deceptive influence over the world. It blinds minds to Christ, captures affections with lesser pleasures, and leaves people confused, fearful, and unable to free themselves. Respectability or order does not remove this bondage, because its effect is spiritual blindness to the light of the gospel.

God’s rescue comes through Jesus Christ, the King who entered life, defeated temptation, and triumphed through the cross. His death broke the devil’s claim and freed believers from slavery to the fear of death. Yet salvation is more than release from captivity. The Father has already brought his people into Christ’s kingdom—a realm of righteousness, peace, joy, truth, and order. Jesus rules with power and love, joins his people to himself, strengthens them in weakness, and keeps them under his care. The sermon therefore calls Christians to resist being governed by feelings during trials, remember God’s blessings, and cultivate thankful joy. Their lives should agree with their words by pursuing Christ as their greatest delight. Those still in darkness are urged to seek mercy from Jesus, the only Saviour able to rescue them and bring them into his kingdom.
28096:
Colossians 1:12 calls Christians to keep giving thanks to the Father who has qualified them to share in the inheritance of the saints in light. This gratitude belongs within a life that pleases God through fruitful work, growing knowledge, patient endurance, and joy. The sermon explains that thankfulness is a pathway to joy: remembering God’s blessings turns the heart from complaint toward contentment and strength. Even amid trials, believers can direct their souls to give thanks and set their minds on blessings that are spiritual and eternal.

The Father is worthy of this gratitude. He is not distant to love, but the source of mercy and comfort whose love was demonstrated by sending his Son. Believers cannot qualify themselves for his inheritance. The Father acted for those without ability, choosing them and drawing them to Christ through a call. He gives each of his people a place in an inheritance that includes eternal life, the coming kingdom, and imperishable blessings kept for them. These gifts are undeserved and received through Christ’s righteousness rather than human merit. The sermon therefore urges Christians to meditate on the Father’s kindness, draw near to him through Jesus, and cultivate thanksgiving. Remembering that he qualified the unqualified can deepen joy, sustain endurance, and shape a life that seeks to please him in everything.
28097:
Philippians 3:15–16 describes the attitude of a growing Christian. Paul admits that he has not reached holiness, yet he refuses to stand still. He presses toward Christ and calls mature believers to share that mindset. Maturity is not sinlessness or merely knowing correct doctrine. It is a continuing life of visible fruit, awareness of sin, love for Jesus, and progress through trials. Suffering can become an opportunity for growth when Christians trust God’s sovereignty, give thanks, and use hardship to advance the gospel rather than retreat into complaint.

This growth begins in the mind. Believers are to adopt the humble, self-giving attitude of Christ, count lesser gains as loss beside knowing him, and protect their thinking from worldly clutter and deception. Scripture, prayer, worship, service, and fellowship train the mind to look toward eternal things. When Christians hold a different attitude from God’s Word, Paul trusts God to reveal and correct it—sometimes through Scripture, other believers, or loving discipline. The mature should therefore remain patient with those who are growing. Finally, believers must keep walking by the standard they have received. The sermon calls listeners to stay on the path of Scripture, follow godly examples, fight sin, seek communion with Christ, value his people, and keep running toward him with their eyes fixed on the finish.
28098:
Colossians 1:9–11 shows that knowing God’s will is meant to transform the whole Christian life. Paul does not pray for knowledge that remains in the mind or produces only impressive discussion. Believers are to be filled with God’s truth so that they walk in a manner worthy of Jesus Christ. This walk follows Jesus, obeys him as Lord when others turn away, and gives devotion to him alone.

The purpose of this walk is to please God in every area of life. Christians do not earn acceptance through good works; they seek to please the Father because Christ has already brought them forgiveness and adoption. Paul identifies two inseparable features of this growth. Believers bear fruit in every good work, persevering through hard circumstances and difficult people with steadfast, joyful patience. They also increase in a personal, intimate knowledge of God, not merely information about him. As they find their deepest delight in his presence, they receive strength to endure and serve without resentment. The sermon calls listeners to study God’s Word deeply, follow Christ with complete obedience, work actively for his kingdom, and seek fellowship with God as their greatest satisfaction. When knowledge leads to loving communion and fruitful action, the Father is honoured and the believer’s life fulfils its intended purpose.
28099:
Paul’s prayer in Colossians 1:9 exposes the difference between true spiritual growth and the counterfeit measures offered by false teachers and a self-centred world. The Colossians were being told that the gospel was not enough and that greater spirituality required philosophy, visions, or special knowledge. Paul instead prayed urgently and persistently that believers would be filled with the knowledge of God’s will, because this is foundational to a life that pleases the Lord and bears fruit.

This knowledge is more than collecting facts or mastering theological language. To be filled is to be governed and directed by God’s will in mind, affection, and action. God has not hidden His will in mystical experiences; believers come to know it by opening, studying, and submitting to His word. Genuine growth is therefore measured not merely by zeal, emotion, comfort, or how much someone knows, but by whether that knowledge shapes faithful obedience.

The sermon calls the church to surrender materialism, personal ambition, and self-protective prayers. Like the believers in Acts who asked for boldness amid real threats, Christians are urged to seek God’s purposes above their own ease. Knowing that they belong wholly to Christ, they can gladly place their plans, possessions, health, and future before God and ask Him to accomplish His will through them.
28100:
The sermon distinguishes a believer’s fixed union with Christ from the fluctuating experience of communion with God. Union rests on God’s saving grace and does not disappear when believers struggle, but communion can weaken because Christians remain prone to wander and fall into sin. This tension should not lead to despair or passivity. Instead, the signs of spiritual battle can remind believers that they need the means God has provided for a deep, living relationship with him. The message therefore urges the church to run to Jesus rather than drifting farther away.

Four practical directions shape that response. Believers run to Christ’s people by gathering, encouraging one another, and resisting isolation. They run to his power through dependent prayer instead of self-reliance, asking for daily provision, forgiveness, and deliverance from temptation. They run to his promises, remembering that Christ nourishes and protects his church while also calling those who have lost their first love to remember and repent. Finally, they run to Christ himself, the gentle and humble Saviour who gives rest and living water. The sermon calls listeners to seek God’s kingdom, use these gracious provisions, and keep returning to Jesus whenever communion grows dry.
28101:
Philippians 3 presents the Christian life as a race requiring determined, lifelong pursuit. Paul had abandoned confidence in his former achievements for the surpassing worth of knowing Christ, yet he still refused to claim that he had reached maturity. His honesty gives believers hope: even an apostle continued to need growth, refinement, and freedom from sin. The response to imperfection is neither complacency nor despair, but pressing forward toward likeness to Christ.

The runner must keep looking ahead. Paul forgets what lies behind, not by denying his past, but by refusing to let former sins, failures, or successes control his course. Because forgiven sin has been dealt with by Christ, believers should repent and continue moving rather than lose momentum by looking back. Earthly ambitions, possessions, work, comfort, and even other people can become weights when they distract from the heavenly goal.

This race is strenuous but not solitary. Christ first laid hold of Paul, gives His people strength, and will bring them to the finish. Christians nevertheless must pursue holiness, exercise self-control, watch their hearts, set their minds on things above, and encourage one another within the church. The sermon therefore calls each listener to examine whether they have entered the race, where their eyes are fixed, and whether their daily ambition is to know and please Christ.
28102:
Paul’s gratitude for the Colossians includes their “love in the Spirit,” love directed toward the saints in their local church. This is not an optional addition to holiness or service. It is the greatest Christian virtue, the bond of unity, and the foundation that gives substance to every gift used for believers’ good. When Christians serve without love, even outwardly impressive activity becomes hollow.

The sermon traces this love to three causes. First, the Holy Spirit gives new birth, making believers children of one Father and drawing them toward others who share the same Christ and indwelling Spirit. Second, the gospel displays Christ’s willing, costly love for the people He redeemed. Those who treasure Him are compelled to honour and care for those whom He loves. Third, hope laid up in heaven loosens the grip of self-love, comfort, possessions, and self-preservation. Looking to Christ enables believers to invest now in the people with whom they will share eternity.

Such love also strengthens the church’s witness. When people of different backgrounds gladly open their homes, sacrifice time and resources, and draw nearer in fellowship, unbelievers see something that self-interest cannot explain. The sermon therefore urges Christians to yield to the Spirit, meditate on the gospel and future hope, and actively meet the needs of their brothers and sisters.
28103:
John 1 announces the wonder that the eternal Word became flesh and lived among us. The sermon explains why Jesus must be both truly God and truly man: his divine nature gives his saving work infinite worth, his humanity makes him a fitting substitute for people, and his experience of temptation enables him to sympathise with human weakness without ever yielding to sin. The incarnation did not mean that the Son ceased to be God. Jesus remains one person with a divine nature and a sinless human nature, and he will remain the God-man for eternity.

From this foundation, the passage presents three great activities of Jesus. He displays God’s glory, not merely as visible brightness, but by revealing God’s truth, love, compassion, mercy, and character. Believers behold that glory in Scripture and are transformed as they receive more of Christ through God’s ordinary means of grace. Jesus also dispenses grace from his inexhaustible fullness: grace that pardons sinners and grace that empowers their growth. Finally, he defines and explains God, making the unseen Father known. Whether life presently feels successful, sorrowful, stressful, or stagnant, the sermon calls listeners to keep seeking Jesus in the Word, worship, prayer, baptism, and the Lord’s Table, receiving from the One who is their Prophet, Priest, and King.
28104:
Paul’s testimony in Philippians 3 shows that becoming a Christian involves more than adopting religious language or avoiding judgment. Before meeting Christ, Paul possessed a heritage, zeal, status, and outward obedience, yet these gave him false confidence. When Christ confronted him, Paul’s assessment changed. Everything he had treated as spiritual gain became loss beside the surpassing worth of knowing Jesus Christ as his Lord.

This change produced a new outcome. Paul no longer sought a righteousness built from his own performance; he wanted to be found in Christ with the righteousness that comes from God through faith. Gaining Christ meant receiving a person, not merely information. Paul desired an intimate, growing knowledge of Jesus, the power of His resurrection, and fellowship with Him even through suffering. His pride and self-reliance gave way to humility, service, gospel proclamation, and endurance.

The sermon asks whether the same transformed priorities are visible in those who profess faith. Work, status, family plans, possessions, comfort, and health are not necessarily wrong, but they must never outweigh Christ or postpone devotion and service. Believers are called to expose their idols, hold everything at God’s disposal, grow in knowing Christ, and willingly follow Him whatever the cost. Those still relying on their own goodness are urged to trust Christ’s finished work rather than their own righteousness.
28105:
Philippians 3 warns against the confidence of being “almost” a Christian. Paul possessed every religious credential his opponents valued: circumcision, Israelite ancestry, an honoured tribe, training as a Pharisee, fierce zeal, and an outwardly blameless record. If heritage, ceremonies, biblical knowledge, sincerity, or moral effort could bring someone into God’s kingdom, Paul would have qualified. Yet Christ was missing, so his confidence remained false.

The warning reaches beyond obvious irreligion. Someone may attend church, grow up in a Christian family, recite Scripture, receive baptism, teach the Bible, show temporary excitement, or perform ministry and still lack new birth. Zeal proves little when its direction is wrong, and outward respectability cannot reveal the heart. Genuine conversion brings deep change: Christ rules, former confidences lose their saving value, new affections arise, and faith produces a life directed toward Christ, His people, and His gospel.

Listeners are urged to examine the basis of their assurance without pretending they can read another person’s heart. Christians should welcome loving questions about visible spiritual fruit and guard against Pharisaic judgment. Those resting on a past prayer, family background, knowledge, or good behaviour are called to run to Christ, repent, and trust His saving work. Confidence must rest in Christ rather than the flesh.
28106:
Life is brief, fragile, and moving toward eternity. Using passengers on a train, the sermon contrasts people consumed by status, safety, possessions, comfort, or entertainment with the wise person who looks beyond this life. Earthly achievements and belongings will soon lose their value, so believers should make present decisions in light of heaven and make their lives count for eternity.

Epaphras provides the example in Colossians 1. He spoke of Christ by teaching the gospel among people who did not know Him. Christians likewise remain on earth as Christ’s ambassadors, able to tell sinners about mercy while opportunity remains. Yet evangelism alone does not prove godliness. Epaphras was first a slave of Christ and then a faithful servant. His work flowed from belonging wholly to his Master rather than seeking importance or doing God a favour.

Recognising Christ’s ownership changes service into worship. Those who know their weakness depend on their Master for strength, provision, protection, joy, and love; His sufficiency is displayed through their work. Believers are called to speak of Christ, gladly submit their goals to Him, and serve faithfully and sacrificially. Unbelieving listeners are urged not to harden themselves against the gospel, but to come to Christ for forgiveness and new life under a gracious Master.
28107:
Colossians 1 describes the gospel as living good news that is spreading, bearing fruit, and increasing. Paul reminds a young church threatened by false teachers that the gospel is true, authoritative, reliable, and sufficient. It crosses ethnic, cultural, national, and geographical barriers by God’s power. Neither imprisonment, persecution, government, nor spiritual opposition can stop its advance, so believers should cling to it and proclaim Christ.

The gospel does more than communicate information. Through it, God gives new birth and enables sinners to understand His grace in Christ. This inward work produces a changed person rather than temporary religious excitement. The true gospel continually bears fruit: growing love for God and His people, deeper knowledge of God, increasing hatred of sin, and renewed dependence on Christ for cleansing and transforming grace. Struggle may remain, but spiritual life cannot be content with stagnation.

The sermon asks listeners to examine present fruit rather than rest on family background, church involvement, or a past profession. Those who see no change are urged not to hide behind excuses or stop at feeling offended, but to seek God’s mercy and ask for Christ now. Those who see growth should thank God, remove worldly weights, keep running to the cross, and desire that the gospel’s transforming work increase throughout their lives, homes, and church.
28339:
Facing false teachers and a pagan culture, the young Colossian church needed a reliable defence. Paul placed the gospel at the centre because Christ does not need to be completed by philosophy, visions, legal demands, possessions, pleasure, or cultural fashion. The gospel is decisive good news: Jesus Christ gave His life for sinners, conquered death, ascended to heaven, reigns as Lord, and promises to bring His people home.

This message gives confident hope rather than wishful thinking. Christ is the believer’s greatest hope, and heaven also holds resurrection, life without sin or pain, lasting inheritance, and reward for faithful service. Looking toward what God has secured strengthens faith, enlarges love for other Christians, sustains obedience through suffering, and loosens attachment to a passing world. Hope in Christ becomes a foundation for sanctification and endurance.

The sermon also explains how the gospel is received. It is authoritative truth, not a mysterious sensation that arrives only when someone feels sufficiently spiritual. A listener must hear, understand, and learn the message, then believe it and entrust body and soul to Jesus as Savior and Lord. Feelings and growth follow Christ’s saving work; they do not create it. Christians should defend and advance this gospel, while unbelieving listeners are urged to stop defending their own goodness and submit to the truth about Christ.
28340:
Paul calls Christians to rejoice in the Lord even while they face trials, opposition and sorrow. This joy is not a forced smile or a superficial feeling. It is a calm assurance rooted in Christ, given to those whom God has brought from spiritual death to life and welcomed as his children. It grows as believers pray, worship, serve one another and remain close to God’s word.

The sermon also explains why Paul repeatedly warns the Philippians about false teachers. The Judaizers placed confidence in circumcision, religious performance and human effort, but outward religion cannot make anyone right with God. True circumcision is a work of God in the heart. Those who belong to Christ worship by the Spirit, boast in Jesus and refuse to trust their own achievements for acceptance with God.

Listeners are therefore encouraged to examine both their source of confidence and what may be robbing them of joy. Those trusting rituals, knowledge or good works are called to repent and rely on Christ alone. Believers who have lost sight of their joy are urged to seek Christ in Scripture, prayer, fellowship and service. Their circumstances may remain painful, but nothing can separate them from God’s love in Christ, and that assurance gives lasting reason to rejoice.
28342:
Paul’s thanksgiving for the Colossians reveals two foundational signs of genuine conversion: faith in Christ Jesus and love for all the saints. Even while imprisoned, Paul remains grateful because Christ is his supreme treasure. He begins with appreciation before correction, showing pastoral care for believers who will soon need protection from false teaching.

Saving faith is more than knowledge, agreement with Christian ideas or confidence in religious activity. It entrusts the whole person to Jesus Christ as both Saviour and Lord. The believer stops relying on personal righteousness and gladly recognises Christ’s authority, committing life and eternity to him. This faith is inward, but it produces visible love.

That love is not merely affectionate speech or convenient kindness. It is sacrificial, patient and practical service shaped by Christ laying down his life. It must be present now as the direction of a believer’s life, though not yet perfect. Its proper setting is the local church, where care extends beyond family, close friends or people who are easy to love. Listeners are invited to examine whether they truly trust Christ and whether that trust is bearing fruit in generous care for every believer in their church, especially those who are difficult, distant or in need.
28343:
Colossians presents Jesus Christ as supreme and completely sufficient. Its opening identifies Paul as Christ’s authorised apostle, Timothy as his trusted companion, and the recipients as saints and faithful brothers and sisters in Christ. A saint is not an exceptional religious hero but every believer whom Christ has purchased and set apart for God. These believers belonged to a particular local church where they could love, serve and obey the Bible’s commands toward one another.

The historical setting explains why this emphasis mattered. The young church at Colossae faced a mixture of Gnostic speculation and Jewish legalism. One offered acceptance with God through Christ plus special knowledge and angel worship; the other through Christ plus ceremonial works. Both diminished Christ by implying that his person and saving work were insufficient.

Paul answers these errors by directing attention back to Christ. All wisdom and knowledge are found in him; the fullness of deity dwells in him; he rules every authority; and redemption and forgiveness are found in him. Nothing can be added to Jesus as the basis of acceptance with God. Listeners are encouraged to let this enlarged vision of Christ shape their worship and obedience, resist teaching that supplements his finished work, and live as people who belong wholly to him within a faithful local church.
28344:
Before beginning Colossians, the sermon considers the life of its author, the apostle Paul, as an example of devotion to Christ. Saul had education, status and religious zeal, yet he was spiritually blind and violently opposed Jesus’ followers. His encounter with the risen Christ exposed that blindness, and his conversion redirected the whole course of his life. His former ambitions gave way to new desires shaped by Jesus.

Paul’s dominant passion was to know and treasure Christ. He counted former gains as loss so that nothing would hinder deeper fellowship with his Saviour. That love also produced anguish for people who remained without Christ. He willingly surrendered personal rights and adapted to others so that more might hear and believe the gospel. Accordingly, Christ was not only the centre of Paul’s affections but also the great subject of his preaching.

Paul’s commitment was tested by repeated beatings, imprisonment, danger, rejection and loss. He endured because he considered present suffering incomparable with the glory to come and wanted Christ magnified whether he lived or died. Rather than merely admiring him, listeners are called to imitate Paul as he imitated Christ: treasure Jesus above worldly ambition, proclaim him faithfully, love those who are lost, and accept costly obedience with confidence that Christ is worth it.
28346:
Epaphroditus shows what humble Christian service looks like when it happens away from prominence. The Philippian church entrusted him with a long and difficult journey to support Paul in prison. Although little else is known about him, Paul describes him with remarkable warmth: a brother, fellow worker, fellow soldier, messenger and minister. His value did not come from a public position but from using his gifts faithfully for Christ and his people.

Each description reveals part of his character. As a brother, he shared genuine affection and family fellowship. As a worker, he served alongside Paul rather than watching from a distance. As a soldier, he accepted hardship and danger for the gospel. As the church’s messenger and minister, he completed their service to Paul at great personal cost, becoming sick and nearly dying in the work.

His compassion was equally striking. Even while ill, Epaphroditus was distressed because the Philippians were worried about him. Paul, though needing his help, sent him home so that they could rejoice. Their mutual concern models service that seeks another person’s good rather than personal comfort. Believers are urged to fight the good fight together, practise sincere love, meet needs, persevere in hardship and honour servants like him. Every gift can serve Christ, including faithful work that few people notice.
28348:
Timothy provides a living example of the humble, selfless service taught throughout Philippians 2. After ten years alongside Paul, he remained available, teachable and ready to undertake a demanding journey for the Philippian church. Paul hoped in the Lord while making his plans, trusting Christ with his imprisonment and future rather than treating circumstances as his ultimate authority.

Paul commends Timothy as a servant of kindred spirit who was genuinely concerned for the believers’ welfare. Timothy had absorbed Paul’s teaching and shared his affection, gospel convictions and desire to put others first. His concern was sincere rather than performed for appearance, and it contrasted with people who pursued their own interests. Their relationship also shows that Christian discipleship and encouragement are shared work: Timothy learned from Paul, became like him and strengthened him in return.

Timothy’s worth had been proved through years of pressure, service and hardship. Like gold tested by fire, his character had matured while he served with Paul for the advance of the gospel. The church is therefore encouraged to build relationships that form dependable servants, not passive spectators. Believers should ask whether they are available, teachable, concerned for others and willing to endure inconvenience for Christ. Mature disciples also help others grow, support their leaders and seek the church’s spiritual welfare above personal comfort or ambition.
28350:
Psalm 103 calls the whole person to bless the Lord and remember his benefits. David does not wait for an external stimulus to create worship; he addresses his own soul and summons every thought, affection and faculty to praise God’s holy name. This wholehearted worship grows from contemplating who God is—compassionate, gracious, patient, faithful and sovereign—and from refusing the spiritual forgetfulness that lets his goodness slip from view.

The opening verses name five benefits. God pardons every iniquity, removing guilt through Christ’s saving work. He heals the diseases of the soul, giving new sight, desires and strength to follow him. He redeems life from destruction, freeing his people from condemnation. He crowns them with steadfast love and compassion, remaining faithful and meeting their pain with a father’s tenderness. Finally, he satisfies them with good things, above all with lasting fellowship in Christ.

These gifts show that God does not perform an incomplete rescue. He forgives, restores, preserves and satisfies his people, and each benefit gives another reason for sincere praise. Believers are encouraged to preach these truths to their own souls so gratitude shapes their words and lives. Those seeking satisfaction in passing pleasures are called instead to trust Jesus, in whom the sermon locates forgiveness, healing, redemption and enduring life.
28352:
Paul describes his life as a drink offering poured over the Philippians’ sacrifice and service of faith. The picture is one of willing devotion: his life belongs to Christ and is spent for Christ’s people. Imprisonment, hardship and the prospect of death do not make him resentful. Christ has changed him from a man concerned with status and achievement into a servant whose concern is the gospel and the church.

Such service remains genuinely joyful. Paul does not ask the Philippians to pity him; he rejoices that he can be spent for their faith and invites them to share that joy. His circumstances remain painful, but his satisfaction rests in Christ and in seeing believers live for Christ. Sacrifice and service belong together, and when they flow from union with Jesus they produce a joy the world cannot explain.

Paul’s example challenges a culture of receiving without giving. Christians are called to offer themselves as living sacrifices, help the weak and put other believers before personal comfort. They should consider what spiritual legacy their lives are forming: whom they encourage, where they pour out time and energy, and whether others can imitate their devotion. Such service may be costly, but it is not wasted. It honours God, strengthens his church and looks toward the eternal glory that outweighs present affliction.
28353:
The Lord’s Supper regularly marks and renews the life of a local church. If membership establishes a person’s relationship with a particular congregation, communion is the family meal at which members remember why God gathered them. They recall Christ’s body given and his blood shed, proclaiming his death, resurrection, present advocacy and promised return. Its purpose is to exalt Christ by announcing the gospel until he comes.

Communion also expresses the believers’ shared partnership. Sharing one bread declares that many believers are one body in Christ, joined to one another for a common gospel purpose. The ordinance therefore belongs to the gathered local church, not isolated individuals or a preferred private group. It calls the whole congregation to renew practical commitments of love, service and unity.

Paul’s warning to Corinth shows the seriousness of that commitment. Eating in an unworthy manner does not mean participants must regard themselves as sinless or personally worthy. In context, the unworthy manner involved division, favouritism and despising other members while claiming fellowship with Christ. A worthy manner is more than the absence of open hostility; it actively seeks warm, tangible love across the body. Believers should examine whether their conduct matches what the meal proclaims, repair division, cherish Christ’s people and join together in making his gospel known.
28439:
Paul commands believers to do everything without grumbling or disputing. These are not harmless habits. Grumbling voices deep dissatisfaction and mistrust, while disputing nurtures quarrelsome reasoning. Israel’s repeated complaints provide a warning that God takes such conduct seriously. Within a church, these sins damage relationships, feed gossip and division, and contradict the humble service modelled by Jesus.
