Instead, it traces three responses that transform how he faces the same unresolved trial: bring the trouble honestly to God, know God through the trouble, and declare that God stands above the trouble.

David first pours out both the external danger and the inward wound. He then turns his attention from the size of the threat to who God is for him: a surrounding shield, his glory, and the one who lifts his head. That renewed focus allows him to sleep, wake, and speak courageously even before circumstances change. The message urges believers not to seize God’s throne by trying to control every possible outcome, nor to assume that suffering caused by their own failures means God has abandoned them. They are invited to bring their real distress to him, remember the security and honour found in Christ, and make requests shaped by God’s character. Faith grows as trials become occasions to know, trust, and praise the God to whom salvation belongs.
29666:
Psalm 67 asks God for grace, blessing, and the light of his face, but it does not treat those gifts as an end in themselves. The sermon explains that God’s people are blessed so that his way and salvation may be known among all nations. Grace is the doorway because recipients bring no merit of their own, and the highest blessing is to know God’s favour in Jesus Christ. Yet enjoying that favour must not become a private spiritual retreat or a small circle concerned only with personal comfort and family welfare.

The message follows the Psalm’s movement from prayer, to purpose, to product. Believers ask for God’s help so that they can become a flowing stream rather than a stagnant reservoir, carrying the good news of Christ beyond themselves. The desired result is not merely outward religious activity, but people from every nation gladly praising God from transformed hearts. The repeated appeal for all peoples to worship reveals an urgent, affectionate longing rather than bare information. Listeners are challenged to examine whether their prayers and use of God’s gifts serve only their own ease. They are urged to repent of self-centred limits, pray for strength, speak about Christ, and share the Psalmist’s desire that the whole world know salvation and rejoice under his righteous rule.
29667:
Psalm 103 calls a weary soul to pause, rise above daily distraction, and remember the goodness of God. David is not describing an enemy or presenting a complaint; he is speaking to his own soul and summoning every part of himself to bless the Lord. The sermon explains that blessing God means proclaiming his goodness with genuine inward worship rather than offering words while the heart remains occupied elsewhere. Spiritual apathy grows when God’s benefits slip from memory, leaving gratitude to be displaced by pride, control, selfishness, or the pursuit of approval.

David therefore tells his soul to forget none of God’s benefits. The message follows five gifts: God pardons every iniquity, heals the soul’s diseases, redeems life from the pit, crowns his people with loving kindness and compassion, and satisfies them with good things. These benefits are presented as the fruit of Christ’s saving work, not rewards for personal merit. Remembering them is described as preaching the gospel to one’s own soul. Listeners are urged to slow down, deliberately recall God’s mercy, and seek lasting satisfaction in fellowship with Christ rather than in temporary comforts. As gratitude grows, God renews the inner person and carries believers above their trials, moving them to praise him sincerely and let his goodness shape their relationships and conduct.
29668:
Continuing through Peter’s greeting to chosen believers, the sermon focuses on the Holy Spirit’s work in salvation and sanctification. It warns against treating the Spirit as an impersonal force, a controllable source of signs, or a means to personal wealth and comfort. The Holy Spirit is God, the Spirit of truth, the helper sent by the Father, and the one who testifies about Jesus Christ. He inspired Scripture, gave power to Christ’s ministry, and applies God’s saving purpose to believers rather than submitting to human commands.

Peter’s phrase about the sanctifying work of the Spirit describes being set apart, consecrated, and purified for God. The message explains that the Spirit does not merely leave a believer unchanged after salvation. Like a new owner renovating a house, he works continuously to reshape the life he inhabits so that Christ is increasingly reflected. Christians are set apart to obey Jesus, bear spiritual fruit, serve with their gifts, evangelise, help one another, resist sin, and live holy lives. Listeners are therefore urged to seek the Spirit’s guidance through Scripture, depend on him in weakness, submit to his authority, and look for genuine transformation rather than dramatic claims. His work consistently puts the spotlight on Christ and prepares believers to be useful in God’s service.
29732:
Psalm 27 addresses the exhaustion that remains when physical rest cannot heal a weary soul. Holidays and breaks can refresh the body, but the sermon argues that the inner person is renewed only through a deeper pursuit of God. David wrote while facing danger, yet he speaks with confidence because the Lord is personally his light, salvation, and defence. The message develops three practical movements for finding rest in God: be intimate with him, be mindful of his past faithfulness, and be devoted to him without reservation.

Intimacy means more than knowing ideas about God; it is personally relying on Christ for guidance, deliverance, protection, and life. Mindfulness looks back through earlier trials and recognises God’s faithful hand, allowing his past care to shape expectations of the future. Devotion is expressed in David’s desire for one thing: to dwell in God’s presence, behold his beauty, and let every relationship and passion come under his rule. This undivided trust does not remove every hardship or the need for physical rest. It prevents fear and divided loyalties from adding unnecessary weight to the soul. Listeners are invited to hand over the areas they still control, seek Christ continually, and let gratitude turn weariness into confident praise and joy.
29733:
The second half of Psalm 27 addresses the painful experience of trusting God while he seems silent or distant. David’s faith does not make him numb to anguish. He feels unheard, abandoned, confused, and threatened, yet he continues to seek God. The sermon organises his response around four directions: look up by crying to God, look beside by trusting that God remains present, look within for what God is teaching, and look forward to the goodness that God will reveal.

Looking up means approaching God without entitlement and pouring out distress on the basis of grace. Looking beside means correcting feelings of abandonment with God’s promise that he will not forsake his people, even when the closest human relationships fail. Looking within is not endless introspection; it is a humble willingness to ask how a sovereign and loving God is using hardship to expose ruling desires and shape Christlike character. Looking forward gives endurance by fixing hope on God’s future goodness, whether relief comes in this life or the life to come. Waiting for the Lord is therefore active rather than passive. Listeners are urged to keep praying, anchor their thoughts in God’s unchanging character, learn through suffering, resist impulsive or despairing responses, and take courage while trusting his timing.
29734:
Isaiah 7:10–14 announces the sign at the heart of Christmas: a virgin will conceive and bear a son called Immanuel. King Ahaz refuses the sign God offers and seeks security through political power rather than faith. Yet his unbelief cannot prevent God from keeping His redemptive promise through the house of David. The sermon uses this setting to remind Christians that human rulers and circumstances never overturn God’s purpose, and that the God who begins His work will bring it to completion.

The prophecy finds its decisive fulfilment in Jesus. Matthew explains that Mary conceives by the Holy Spirit before coming together with Joseph, so the child is truly human yet without sin. The sign is not Mary herself but the Son she bears—the promised Saviour able to represent His people, sympathise with their weakness, and give His sinless life for them. His name, Immanuel, means “God with us.” Christmas therefore celebrates the eternal Son taking human flesh, living under the law, dying and rising to reconcile sinners to God. In trials, believers can remember that God is not distant but present with them in Christ. The sermon calls hearers to look beyond gifts and traditions, trust the unique Saviour, rejoice in His finished work, and share the good news that eternal life is found in Him.
29735:
Psalm 51 records David’s prayer after Nathan confronted him about adultery and murder. The sermon uses his response to describe genuine repentance as reliance, eradication, and motivation. Repentance begins with reliance on God’s grace, not an attempt to become respectable before approaching him. David does not minimise his guilt or appeal to his achievements. He asks for mercy according to God’s loving kindness and compassion, and the message directs Christians to depend entirely on the cleansing secured through Jesus Christ.

Grace does not excuse continued sin. David asks God to blot out his transgressions, wash him thoroughly, and cleanse him. These images address the record of guilt, the inward defilement sin produces, and the need to be restored to communion with God. His motivation is an honest acknowledgment of the enormity of his sin, the God against whom he has sinned, and the corrupt desires from which sinful actions arise. He refuses blame-shifting and asks for truth in the innermost being. Listeners are urged to move beyond shallow confession of visible behaviour and ask God to expose the pride, control, selfishness, or other ruling desires beneath it. Genuine repentance runs toward grace, seeks the complete removal of sin, and longs above all for renewed fellowship with God.
29763:
Peter’s greeting to scattered believers reaches its climax in Jesus Christ. The Father chooses, the Holy Spirit sets people apart, and this saving work has a purpose: obedience to Jesus and cleansing through his blood. The sermon rejects the idea that election is merely a label or that grace leaves a person unchanged. Christian obedience does not earn salvation, nor is it flawless, but it reveals a heart made alive by God. Those who truly love Christ increasingly desire his holiness, serve his people, proclaim the gospel, and turn from former desires even when obedience is costly or opposed.

This response begins with seeing who Jesus is. He is the eternal Son who became truly human, bore sin, rose, reigns, and is worthy of worship and allegiance. The more believers grasp his glory and love, the more obedience becomes grateful devotion rather than legalistic burden. Peter’s reference to sprinkling with blood recalls Israel’s covenant commitment to obey after hearing God’s Word. In the new covenant, Christ’s shed blood assures his faithfulness to cleanse and keep his people, while those he saves belong to him in obedient loyalty. The sermon calls listeners to examine whether their claimed love for Jesus is visible in conduct, relationships, service, and witness, while directing unbelievers first to bow to Christ and receive his saving mercy.
29764:
Peter encourages persecuted believers by directing their hope beyond the grave. After teaching about the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, he breaks into praise because God has caused his people to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The sermon stresses that theology should become doxology: learning who God is should move the mind, will, and heart to worship him in good circumstances and in suffering. Scripture is not studied merely to collect information or identify error, but to know Christ and become more devoted to him.

The message contrasts this living hope with every promise of the present world. Health, possessions, status, appearance, and comfort fade, while Christians may face temptation, hardship, and persecution. Their inheritance is different: it is imperishable, undefiled, unfading, reserved in heaven, and protected by God’s power. This hope rests on God’s great mercy and Christ’s resurrection rather than human achievement. Because Jesus rose, believers can look forward with certainty rather than wishful thinking. Listeners are therefore asked where their hope truly lies. They are urged to resist blending into the world, study Scripture to know Christ, praise God for his mercy, and endure present trials with their eyes fixed on the salvation and inheritance still to be fully revealed.
29765:
Continuing through Psalm 51, the sermon moves from genuine repentance to genuine restoration. Repentance turns away from sin, but restoration renews fellowship with God, reshapes the life, and produces fruit. David first asks to hear joy and gladness because sin has left him with bone-crushing misery. The message explains that temptation first promises pleasure and then uses guilt to drive the believer farther from God. Christ answers both lies: he is better than sin’s fleeting offer, and his mercy is greater than the guilt that follows.

Restoration therefore begins with renewed joy in God’s salvation. David then asks for a clean heart and a steadfast spirit, recognising that only God can bring order and life out of inward chaos. A transformed heart remains focused on Christ, longs for God’s presence, and finds delight rather than mere duty in following him. That inward renewal produces visible fruit: testimony to others, joyful praise, and authentic worship. David’s broken and contrite heart shows that restoration does not leave repentance behind. He remains honest about the enormity of sin and depends on God’s grace rather than empty religious activity. Listeners are urged to reject condemning lies, cling to Christ’s mercy, seek deep inner renewal, and let restored joy overflow in witness, praise, and humble worship.
29783:
Psalm 100 presents genuine worship as the fitting response of people who have been brought through repentance and restoration. The sermon traces three connected features of that worship: it is joyful, rooted in knowing God, and overflowing with thanksgiving. Joy is not manufactured by music, atmosphere, or spectacle. It grows as believers understand who the Lord is: the sovereign God who made them, owns them, cares for them as his sheep, and reveals himself as their faithful Shepherd. Such knowledge moves worship beyond reluctant duty into glad service, singing, praise, and delight in belonging to Jesus Christ.

The message then calls believers to enter worship with gratitude because the Lord is good, his lovingkindness is everlasting, and his faithfulness continues through every generation. Worship is not a favour offered to a needy God; it is the response of needy people who receive from a generous King. The sermon therefore urges listeners to repent of treating gathered worship as a chore or withdrawing whenever they feel weary. Instead, they are invited to come with their need, receive strength from the knowledge of God, and carry that joy into trials, family pressures, and temptations. Genuine worship leaves believers steadied by the Shepherd’s care and ready to face life with thankful confidence in him.
29784:
Using Paul’s picture of an athlete in 1 Corinthians 9, this sermon urges believers to run the Christian race with purpose, discipline, and their eyes fixed on Christ. The call is for every Christian, not merely leaders or unusually gifted people. Life brings weariness, distractions, temptation, and responsibilities that can obscure the goal, yet believers are not spectators. They are called to persevere, lay aside what entangles them, and remember that Christ awaits them at the finish. Examples from Hebrews—such as Enoch, Noah, and Moses—show ordinary and imperfect people trusting God, walking with him, obeying his word, and valuing his promised reward above present comfort.

The sermon explains that running well requires aim and self-control. Like an athlete training for a prize, a believer must bring hindering habits and bodily desires under discipline rather than excuse them. Paul’s concern about disqualification is presented as a warning against hypocritical Christian living, not as the loss of salvation. His own suffering demonstrates that exhaustion and hardship need not end faithful service. The message invites listeners to identify whatever is slowing them down, draw near to Christ, and keep moving—even when progress feels like crawling—until they finish the course. Those outside the race are called to trust the crucified and risen Jesus, the only way to the Father.
29785:
Psalm 133 celebrates the goodness and pleasure of God’s people dwelling together in unity. This sermon explains that biblical unity is more than occupying the same room or attending the same service. It is a Christ-centred commitment in which believers genuinely delight in one another, share life, forgive, counsel, serve, weep, and rejoice together. Such fellowship is both good for the soul and pleasant to the heart because it displays the character of Jesus through his people. The psalm’s picture of precious oil flowing down Aaron’s garments points to unity as a gift that comes from God and consecrates Christ’s body for a shared purpose.

The image of dew reaching from Mount Hermon to dry Mount Zion shows the refreshing blessing that flows through a united church. God supplies encouragement, comfort, counsel, and service through the varied gifts of believers, so isolation cuts people off from benefits Christ intends them to receive through his body. Their common life also carries the aroma of the gospel, showing the world something of God’s love, kindness, forgiveness, and care. The sermon calls the church to protect this unity from gossip, false teaching, selfish isolation, and indifference while actively strengthening it through hospitality, humble help, devotion, and sacrifice. Because Christ loves his church, his people should treasure and cultivate their life together.
29786:
Beginning with the story of a young man sinking in quicksand, this sermon asks how believers can find true rest and renew their hearts when trials, illness or besetting sin seem to pull them under. The answer is found in Isaiah 42:16, from the "book of consolation", where God declares five times what he will do: lead the blind, guide them, turn darkness into light, smooth rugged places and not leave them undone. First, the sovereignty of God. Isaiah's precise prophecies of judgment by Assyria and Babylon, and of Cyrus decades before his birth, show that God is the author of history. They comforted the exiles and point to the Messiah who will return to reign, so believers can rest in his righteous right hand.

Second, the power of God. The blind who did not know the way describes every believer before conversion, like a man at a Japanese shrine drawing curse after curse. Regenerating a depraved heart displays God's power even more than creating the universe, and that same power upholds his people. Third, the remembrance of God. Because his people are prone to forget him (Deuteronomy 6:12), believers must deliberately remember the Lord in prosperity, in adversity and in despair, making Christ their one pursuit as Paul did. Even a faith hanging by a thread is held because Christ spun it. Unbelievers are urged to repent and believe.
29788:
In Exodus 3, Moses asks two questions: “Who am I?” and, in effect, “Who is God?” After forty years as a prince of Egypt and forty in obscurity as a shepherd, Moses sees his age, failure, and lack of resources and feels inadequate to confront Pharaoh. God does not rebuild Moses’ self-confidence. He answers, “I will be with you,” directing Moses away from both pride and despair and toward the character of the One who will accomplish the rescue. The sermon applies this contrast to believers who may alternate between self-reliance and fear: identity, purpose, and confidence must be rooted in knowing God rather than measuring personal ability.

God’s name, “I am who I am,” reveals him as self-existent, independent, unchanging, eternal, and incomparable. Every creature depends on him for life and movement, while he depends on nothing and possesses the fullness of his being. This transcendent God comes near in grace, keeps his promises, and reveals himself in Jesus Christ. The message follows that revelation to the cross, where the great I Am willingly gives himself for sinners and rises again. Believers are invited to receive awareness of their insufficiency as a grace, rest confidently in God’s sufficiency, and trust his presence and purposes. Unbelievers are urged to turn to Jesus while there is time.
29789:
First Peter teaches that Christians can know deep joy before the grave, even while they endure painful trials. This joy is not the absence of sorrow, persecution or difficulty, and it is not controlled by changing circumstances. It begins with salvation: through Jesus Christ, believers have received mercy, new life, a living hope and an imperishable inheritance kept in heaven. Their joy is rooted in Christ rather than in their performance or visible fruit. Trials are purposeful and temporary within God’s care. They test the genuineness of faith, refine believers as fire refines gold, and reveal that God is continuing his work in them.

The sermon describes joy in salvation, sanctification and expectation. Christians can rejoice in what Christ has already given, in the refining work God performs through present difficulties, and in the praise, glory and honour awaiting them when Jesus is revealed. This does not deny grief or weakness; Peter himself stumbled, yet his faith endured and grew. Listeners are encouraged to examine how they respond to trials, return from sin that has diminished their joy, and keep trusting Jesus. Above all, Christian joy belongs with love for Christ: believers have not seen him, yet they love and trust him. Those without that love are urged to ask Jesus for a new heart and salvation.
29790:
Opening a series through Luke’s Gospel, this sermon introduces both Luke’s distinctive portrait of Jesus and the certainty on which Christian faith rests. Matthew presents the promised King, Mark emphasizes the obedient servant, and John declares the Son of God; Luke especially portrays the Son of Man whose compassion reaches sinners, outsiders, sufferers, and the lost. Scenes unique to Luke reveal that compassion, including the father welcoming the prodigal son, Jesus praying for his executioners, and his care for people in distress. Yet the message asks an essential question: how can readers know these events are more than religious stories?

Luke’s prologue answers through the source, means, and purpose of his account. Its source is the testimony of many firsthand witnesses who saw Jesus’ works, heard his teaching, and served the message they received. Its means is Luke’s careful investigation of everything from the beginning and his deliberate arrangement of the material. Its purpose is that readers may know the certainty of what they have been taught. The sermon therefore rejects faith as a blind leap and presents Luke as a researched, trustworthy account of Jesus’ life, death, and resurrection. That certainty is intended to reshape life: listeners are called to anchor themselves in Christ, follow him despite opposition, cherish his compassion, and boldly share the truth about him.
29795:
Luke begins his account of Jesus’ coming with the promised birth of John the Baptist, revealing God’s faithfulness after four centuries of prophetic silence. Israel lived under political oppression and widespread spiritual corruption, yet God had not forgotten his covenant. Zechariah and Elizabeth embody that message: their names together recall that the Lord remembers his promise, while their righteous and devoted lives stand out amid religious hypocrisy. Their long barrenness, however, had brought grief, shame, and the apparent loss of hope. The sermon follows Zechariah into the temple, where a once-in-a-lifetime priestly privilege becomes the moment God breaks the silence.

An angel announces that Zechariah’s prayer has been heard and that Elizabeth will bear a son named John. Their private sorrow becomes part of God’s larger answer to Israel, because John will prepare the way for the promised Messiah. The message emphasizes that God’s delay is not denial: he remains at work even when circumstances are dark and his purposes cannot yet be seen. His faithfulness is grounded in his own character rather than in the worthiness of his people. Listeners facing discouragement or long-unanswered prayer are therefore urged to resist anxious striving, wait on God, trust his control, and believe that he hears his children and acts in his perfect time and way.
29798:
First Peter describes believers who love and trust Jesus although they have not seen him. This sermon explores unseen faith as encouragement and a test of genuine Christianity. Sight is insufficient to create faith: people saw Jesus’ miracles, heard him, and even touched him yet still rejected him. Biblical faith instead comes through hearing the word of Christ and is shown when believers continue loving and trusting Jesus amid persecution, sorrow, sickness, and trials. Such love is not a passing emotion, an earned exchange, or a response dependent on favourable circumstances. It is God’s work in the heart and rests on knowing who Jesus is.

The message gives reasons to love and trust Christ: he loved sinners first, gave himself for them, intercedes for his people, remains with them, supplies his Spirit, and works even suffering for their good. That trust produces inexpressible joy and an enduring, undivided love that becomes visible in ordinary relationships. Love for Jesus is expressed through patience under pressure, kindness toward difficult people, forgiveness, hospitality, service, generosity, fellowship, and care for both believers and neighbours. Listeners are urged to examine whether their love for Christ is growing, deepen it through Scripture, prayer, worship, and fellowship, and turn from competing loves. Those who do not know Christ are called to repent and come to him now.
29800:
Working through Luke 1:18-25, this sermon examines what happens when unbelief collides with God's promises. What keeps a sinner from Christ is not the size of his sin but unbelief, for one cry of faith is enough. Even for believers, doubting God's word insults his character and invites his fatherly discipline. First, unbelief questions God's integrity. Zechariah, a righteous priest standing in the holy place before an angel, measured God's promise of a son against his own age and his wife's barrenness, though he knew how God had opened the wombs of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah. Believers do the same when they give up praying for an unsaved relative or accept defeat by a besetting sin, making Christ look small and their problems large.

Second, unbelief brings God's discipline. Gabriel, whose name proclaims God's might, struck Zechariah mute and deaf until the promise was fulfilled, removing him from his ministry. This was not punishment for sin, which Christ bore, but the correction of a loving Father. Third, unbelief cannot stop God's grace. Elizabeth conceived, and while her doubting husband was silent she praised the Lord for taking away her disgrace. Christians are urged to confess their unbelief, believe what God has said and follow Elizabeth's example rather than Zechariah's.
29801:
Gabriel’s announcement to Mary reveals the grace of Jesus’ arrival, the glory of his person, and the grandeur of his reign. Heaven’s King does not enter through palaces or prestigious families but comes to an unknown village and a woman with no status. Mary is called favoured because she receives undeserved grace, not because she dispenses it. This setting shows that Christ comes for the weak, insignificant, needy, and sinful. No one is too small or too far gone to receive the grace of the King who comes down to save.

The promised child is human, conceived in Mary’s womb, yet he is also the Son of the Most High who shares the nature and greatness of God. His name, Jesus, declares his saving mission. As God and man in one person, he can represent humanity, bear the sinner’s punishment, and reconcile people to God. The angel also announces that he is David’s rightful heir whose kingdom will never end. The sermon looks forward to Christ’s unopposed reign of justice, peace, renewal, and blessing. Believers are called to bow, trust, worship, remove distractions, and honour this majestic King now. Those who have not trusted him are invited to come without relying on their own works, because Jesus has paid the price and is able to save and transform them.
29802:
Mary’s response to the angel pictures faith receiving God’s word and bearing visible fruit. Unlike Zechariah’s demand for certainty, Mary asks how the virgin conception will occur while accepting that it will. Gabriel directs her to God’s power: the Holy Spirit will overshadow her, and the child will be the holy Son of God. Jesus is human and divine, conceived without an earthly father or sin. Although the mystery exceeds ordinary explanation, God does not require Mary to comprehend everything. He calls her to believe what he has said concerning his Son.

Mary answers as the Lord’s servant, receiving the promise without bargaining, delay, or claims of personal worthiness. This illustrates saving faith as resting on God’s word and welcoming Christ rather than accumulating good deeds or first overcoming every sin. Such receiving faith begins a new life and produces fruit. Mary immediately seeks fellowship with Elizabeth; John leaps for joy in Christ’s presence; Elizabeth celebrates under the Spirit’s influence; and both women rest in assurance that God fulfils his word. The sermon calls believers to resist unbelief, renew trust in God’s promises, pursue unity, rejoice in Christ, and speak of him with Spirit-shaped confidence. Those who do not know Christ are invited to come as they are and receive the risen Saviour by faith.
29804:
Mary’s praise in Luke 1:46–50 directs attention away from herself and toward Jesus Christ. Though she is a young, obscure servant, she rejoices in “God my Saviour” and magnifies the Lord who has looked on her lowly condition. Her blessing does not arise from personal holiness or social importance, but from the mighty Saviour dwelling within her. The sermon therefore invites every believer to join Mary, receive Christ with empty hands, and let inward joy become public praise rather than private, silent feeling.

Mary celebrates three divine perfections in the Saviour: his might, holiness, and mercy. His power accomplishes what is impossible, defeats sin and death, and can soften the hardest heart. His holiness means that he is beautiful beyond comparison and worthy of wholehearted worship. His mercy bends toward guilty, undeserving people, reaches through every generation, and is seen most clearly in Christ. The fear of God mentioned in Mary’s song is not a price that earns mercy; it is the awed response mercy creates in those who have received it. Listeners are called to turn from apathy and complacency, fix their attention on the mighty, holy, merciful Saviour, speak of him openly, and receive him by faith without presenting personal merit as a qualification.
29805:
Peter’s words in 1 Peter 1:10–12 encourage suffering believers to recognise the treasure they already possess in Christ. The prophets spoke about the grace, sufferings, and coming glories of the Messiah, yet searched their own writings to understand the person and time being revealed. Their witness shows that salvation is not a recent invention: God’s purpose runs through Scripture and reaches fulfilment in Jesus Christ. Believers now stand in a privileged place because they know the crucified and risen Saviour whom the prophets anticipated.

The sermon presents Scripture as God’s inspired word, given through prophets and apostles by the Holy Spirit. Those earlier servants were ministering for the benefit of later believers, and even angels long to look into this salvation. Therefore, Christians facing trials should not hunt for lasting satisfaction in the world. They should esteem salvation, find joy, comfort, rest, and future hope in Christ, and search the Bible to know him rather than merely accumulate information. The same Spirit who worked through the prophets now dwells in believers, and the church is called to proclaim reconciliation through Christ. Unbelieving listeners are urged to seek Jesus in Scripture, asking God to reveal the Saviour to whom the whole message points.
29806:
Mary’s praise in Luke 1:51–55 reveals how differently God judges greatness. Jesus entered the world in poverty and apparent weakness, yet stands at the centre of history. In the same way, God scatters those who are proud in the thoughts of their hearts, brings rulers down, and exposes every attempt to build identity on status, talent, wealth, or recognition. His concern reaches beneath outward service to the self-sufficient thoughts that resist correction and imagine they can stand without him.

God also lifts the humble and fills the spiritually hungry with good things. Humility is not timidity, shyness, or lack of confidence. It is coming to the end of self-dependence, accepting spiritual bankruptcy, and approaching God with empty hands. The good gift that satisfies such hunger is ultimately Christ himself, the bread of life. God helps his covenant people not because humility earns favour, but because he remembers his mercy. Jesus embodies that mercy and offers salvation to undeserving sinners. Trials may therefore expose pride and teach believers to cling to Christ again. The sermon calls listeners to stop defending their own sufficiency, admit their need, cooperate with God’s humbling work, and trust that those who rest in Christ will be filled with his grace and finally lifted with him in glory.
29807:
The birth and naming of John in Luke 1:56–66 display grace that gives beyond expectation. Grace is God’s unearned gift to people who deserve the opposite, not mere leniency or a reward for improvement. It arrives according to God’s time and is not defeated by long delay, human impossibility, or spiritual barrenness. Elizabeth’s unexpected son turns public shame into honour, while the name John—“Yahweh is gracious”—announces that God’s purpose outranks family custom and inherited identity.

Zechariah’s obedience in naming the child is followed by restored speech and eruptive praise. The surrounding community moves from gossip and judgment to holy awe, and news of God’s mercy spreads through the countryside. Grace therefore cannot be hoarded: when it truly changes a person, it produces gratitude, worship, freedom from man-made traditions, and an outward effect on other believers. Yet John is not the final subject. His life and name point to Jesus Christ, the Lamb of God who brings grace upon grace. The sermon urges believers to recognise the greater grace they have received in Christ, let it reshape everyday identity and decisions, speak of him openly, and live as grateful followers rather than returning to cultural restrictions, habitual sin, or a sense of entitlement.
29821:
Exodus 17 presents Israel’s crisis at Rephidim, their accusation and God’s grace. God deliberately leads his people to a place without water, not to ruin them, but to expose their self-reliance and teach them to depend on the giver rather than his gifts. Instead, Israel quarrels with Moses, demands water, questions whether the Lord is present and places God on trial. Their response warns that suffering can harden the heart when people reinterpret God’s past goodness, judge his motives and demand that he act on their terms. A waterless place is not proof that God has abandoned his people; it may be where he is forming deeper trust.

God answers with a courtroom scene. Moses brings the elders as witnesses and carries the staff of judgment, yet God stands identified with the rock and commands Moses to strike it. Judgment falls on the rock, while undeserving people receive life-giving water. The sermon traces this image through Scripture to Jesus Christ, the rock who bears judgment at the cross and gives living water to his people. Christians facing trials are urged to look to the cross rather than accuse God. Prayer, Scripture and encouragement within the church help them remember that God remains good, present and dependable, and that he is teaching them to rely on him.
29822:
The sermon explores the manifold mercy of God as the attribute that makes a holy God approachable to broken sinners. Mercy is God’s tender, compassionate care for people ruined by sin. His general mercy reaches across creation: he restrains judgment, shows patience, warns sinners, and gives them time to turn to Christ. This kindness must not be treated as permission to continue in sin, because the opportunity to receive mercy in this life will not last forever.

God’s sovereign mercy is his saving compassion toward his people. It is not grounded in righteous deeds or personal sorrow, but in God’s own freedom and loving purpose. The message describes this mercy as salvific, undeserved, great, and parental. It rescued violent opponents such as Paul, continues to care for believers who stumble, and sometimes disciplines them rather than abandoning them. Because God is rich in mercy, his children should run toward him when guilty instead of hiding as though he were reluctant to receive them. The cross displays the depth of his compassion and assures sinners that abundant mercy is found in Jesus. Unbelievers are urged to seek that mercy while there is opportunity; believers are called to enjoy it, praise God for it, and extend mercy to others rather than hoarding what they have received.
29823:
Zechariah’s prophecy in Luke 1 is presented as a song of praise, not merely a lesson about how salvation works. The preacher invites listeners to behold Jesus as a compassionate savior, a loving redeemer and a mighty king. He also pauses over Zechariah being filled with the Holy Spirit: praise that honours Christ is the fitting response to God’s work, and believers are urged to yield to the Spirit’s guidance.

God’s visit to his people means decisive intervention, not a casual call. The preacher traces earlier acts of deliverance before describing Jesus coming personally into a world marked by sin and self-righteousness. Redemption is pictured as release from slavery through a costly purchase: Christ’s death frees his people from sin’s penalty and gives them freedom to resist its power. The “horn of salvation” then points to royal strength, seen in Christ’s victory and anticipated in his future reign.

This praise calls for more than distant admiration. Believers are encouraged to resist sin, delight in Christ and give him their daily lives. Those who do not know him are invited to come helplessly and rest in his saving power rather than trust their own works.
29824:
At the close of Zechariah’s prophecy in Luke 1, the preacher focuses on the tender mercy of God. This is not presented as reluctant kindness extracted from a distant God. He describes mercy as flowing from God’s own heart and gives three images for its work in Jesus: mercy visits, shines and guides. The sunrise from on high is identified with Christ, who comes into a world unable to find its own way out of darkness.

The message says that mercy is both the reason Jesus came and the manner of his coming. Rather than arriving in display of force, he came humbly. He shines on people sitting in spiritual darkness and under death’s shadow; the preacher points to the cross as the decisive answer to that darkness. Christ then guides his people along their daily way towards peace with God, not merely towards a distant destination.

Listeners are asked to reject two mistaken pictures of mercy: that God gives it grudgingly when they sin, or that suffering proves he has none for them. The preacher calls believers to look to Christ’s cross, run towards God rather than away from him, and seek their satisfaction in his mercy.
29825:
In Luke 2:1–7, the preacher sees the birth of Jesus through three connected themes: God’s sovereignty, the wonder of his providence and the humility of the incarnation. Luke names rulers, a census and places to present the birth as an event in history. Caesar’s decree appears to display imperial power, yet the preacher argues that it also serves God’s purpose by bringing Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem. No earthly ruler stands above the Lord who directs the outcome.

The message then moves from Rome to an ordinary couple. Joseph’s journey from Nazareth shows the preacher how God works through unremarkable people and everyday circumstances, not only spectacular signs. Bethlehem and Joseph’s connection to David matter to his account of the promised king. The birth itself is strikingly humble: Mary gives birth in ordinary human conditions, wraps her son in cloths and lays him in a manger because there is no room for them. The preacher presents this as the Son of God sharing human frailty rather than arriving in visible splendour.

He calls listeners to worship God above human powers, trust his care even through hardship, and answer Jesus’ humility by setting aside pride and treating others with gentleness.
29826:
In 1 Peter 1:13, the preacher turns from what believers have received in Christ to how they should live as pilgrims. Peter's commands are grounded in the new birth and living hope he has already described, not offered as a way to earn salvation. Even when illness, persecution or family troubles make life difficult, Christians are called to fix their hope completely on the grace Jesus will bring when he appears. The sermon invites listeners to look beyond passing comforts and remember that Christ's return and the promised life with him give them a reason to persevere with joy.

That expectation calls for an active mind and a sober spirit. The preacher explains Peter's image of preparing the mind for action as gathering up what is loose and distracting so that thoughts can be directed by God's truth. Sobriety means alert self-control rather than drifting through life or being drawn away by fear, temptation and everyday distractions. Believers are encouraged to dwell on Scripture, pray for its truth to shape their hearts, and live expectantly in obedience and witness. Those who do not yet have Christ as their hope are urged to come to him for mercy and a new heart.
29831:
The preacher asks whose character a Christian's life reflects. Working hard, improving a home or admiring another person is not the problem; the danger is making the world's desires and approval one's aim. Turning to Peter's call to holiness, he says believers are passing through this world and should not return to the passions that shaped their lives before they knew Christ. Holiness means being set apart from sin and devoted to what is right. This is not a method of earning salvation. Peter addresses people already called God's obedient children and urges them to live out the change God has begun in them.

The sermon then moves from the negative command not to conform to former desires to the positive call to resemble the holy God who called them. The preacher draws on other biblical passages to contrast an old way of life with renewed minds and new conduct. Holiness is therefore more than avoiding wrongdoing: it involves speech, relationships, witness and everyday choices, at home as well as at church. Listeners are encouraged to resist worldly temptations, cultivate humility, stay near God's word and let their lives point others to Christ. Those who do not know him are invited to seek him rather than imitate the world.
29832:
In Luke's account of the shepherds who hear of Jesus' birth, the preacher traces a movement from fear to joy and from hearing to action. The shepherds are portrayed as people of low standing, startled by the angel and God's glory. The angel's announcement is good news for them: a Saviour, Christ the Lord, has been born. The preacher dwells on those titles to explain why the child is the source of joy, and on the manger to show the humility of one who comes near to the lowly. He urges listeners to know themselves truthfully before God and receive Christ joyfully rather than trusting their own importance.

The sermon then follows the shepherds' response. They hear the heavenly praise, go promptly to see the child, tell others what they were told, and return glorifying God. The preacher distinguishes mere amazement from Mary's treasuring and pondering of these events, inviting a response that reaches the heart and changes priorities. He calls believers to praise Christ, seek him eagerly and proclaim him without shame. Reluctance to share the good news, he suggests, may call for renewed humility and deeper delight in the Saviour rather than simply more confidence in one's own ability.
29834:
Returning to Zechariah's prophecy in Luke 1, the preacher asks why God visits and redeems his people through Christ. He follows four movements in the song: God shows mercy, remembers his covenant, graciously grants rescue and service, and gives forgiveness. Mercy is striking because the people have sinned against God, yet he draws near rather than leaving them. Remembering the oath to Abraham does not mean that God had forgotten it; the preacher understands it as God's faithful action to fulfil his promise. He presents Jesus as the one through whom that promised blessing comes.

Rescue, the sermon says, has a positive purpose as well as deliverance from enemies: God's people are freed to serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness, throughout their lives. Zechariah's words about his child John then point beyond John to Jesus, because John's mission is to prepare people for salvation through the forgiveness of sins. The preacher stresses that pardon is central, not an afterthought to hopes for political deliverance. Rather than ending with a long list of tasks, he invites listeners to meditate on these gifts, delight in the Saviour and answer with grateful praise. Remembering God's mercy and faithfulness should shape their response even in trials.
29907:
In 1 Peter 1:17, the preacher considers what it means for believers to address God as Father while knowing that he judges impartially according to each person's work. He first dwells on the closeness and care of the Father who hears his children in suffering. That relationship should not make them casual about his holiness or their conduct. The sermon distinguishes the believer's reverent fear from terror of condemnation: it is awe, love and respect that lead a child to honour the Father. The preacher also discusses judgment and future rewards, urging listeners not to spend their lives pursuing only what passes away.

Peter's command to conduct themselves in fear during their stay becomes a call to live as sojourners with eternity in view. The preacher uses the picture of a child entrusted with a father's household to challenge complacency: receiving love and an inheritance is no reason to ignore the father's wishes. He encourages practical faithfulness in loving others, generosity, humility and witness, even through hardship. Such service is not presented as a way to escape condemnation, but as the response of those who belong to God and seek to finish well. He closes by warning those who do not know God as Father to turn to Christ.
29908:
In Luke's account of Simeon meeting the infant Jesus, the preacher sees another witness to the promised Christ. Simeon is introduced without an important public office, yet he is righteous and devout, waiting for Israel's consolation and guided by the Holy Spirit. The preacher holds up his character, longing, reception of Jesus and prayer as a pattern worth considering. He explains Simeon's righteousness as received through faith rather than earned by a tally of good deeds, and his devotion as an active hunger for God. The Spirit's promise that Simeon would see the Christ gives his waiting a clear focus.

When Jesus is brought into the temple, Simeon takes him into his arms and blesses God. He can speak of departing in peace because, in the preacher's reading, he has seen God's salvation in the person of Jesus. Simeon's prayer looks beyond himself to light for Gentiles and glory for Israel. The sermon therefore calls listeners not merely to admire Jesus from a distance but to receive and treasure him. It also challenges the assumption that usefulness to God depends on worldly status. Like this otherwise little-known man, believers are urged to long for Christ, remain faithful in ordinary life and find peace in him even when facing loss and death.
29909:
Continuing Luke's account of Jesus' presentation at the temple, the preacher considers Mary and Joseph's amazement at Simeon's words. He says the child's identity and mission are still unfolding before them: Jesus is God's salvation, and Simeon's earlier prayer reaches beyond Israel to the Gentiles. Yet amazement alone is only a beginning. Simeon's further words announce that the child will be opposed and will bring both falling and rising. The preacher understands this as a division made visible in people's response to Jesus. Even Mary will suffer deeply as opposition to her son reaches its terrible height, and that opposition exposes what is in human hearts.

The sermon then turns to Anna, whose long devotion is expressed in prayer, fasting, thanksgiving and telling others about the child. Her faithfulness offers a contrast to mere wonder or resistance. The preacher asks listeners not simply to be impressed by Christ, but to receive him and remain devoted to him. He challenges the idea that service can wait until a comfortable retirement or must stop with old age. Anna's example encourages both younger and older believers to serve with what they can do, including prayer and witness, and to finish their lives faithfully rather than drift into self-centred ease.
29912:
The preacher follows Luke from the close of Jesus' quiet youth into the opening of John the Baptist's ministry. Luke names powerful political and religious figures, yet the word of God comes to John in the wilderness. The preacher draws from this contrast a reminder that God does not need status, wealth or influence to carry out his saving purpose. John is sent to prepare people for the coming king, not by repairing literal roads but by preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. The message asks what must change in a heart for that king to be welcomed.

The preacher explains forgiveness as a debt cancelled through Christ, not God pretending sin never happened. In this sermon, repentance means abandoning reliance on personal effort as a way to be right with God and turning one's trust to Jesus; baptism publicly declares that change. Isaiah's imagery of straight paths, filled valleys and lowered hills becomes a picture of obstacles such as unbelief, guilt and pride being removed. The preacher insists that this work is beyond human self-polishing and calls hearers to approach Christ with empty hands. Both those first receiving him and believers seeking to grow are urged to let go of self-reliance and depend on the generous king.
29960:
Preaching from 1 Peter 1:22–25, the preacher asks what Christian love looks like and whom this command addresses. Peter calls believers to love one another fervently from the heart, not to offer a pleasant greeting while privately withholding affection. The sermon contrasts that sincere, active love with a self-interested exchange that gives only when something is returned. It focuses especially on love among brothers and sisters in the church, where different people must actually care for one another through trials rather than speak vaguely of loving a distant community. This love should be offered without favouritism, including to someone a listener finds difficult to love.

The preacher grounds the command in new birth through God's living and enduring word. He says believers do not manufacture this kind of love by themselves; Christ's love and God's work in them make it possible, while they still must obey and grow. Because the word that brought them life endures when human glory fades, its fruit should remain visible. The sermon gives practical shape to love through patience, kindness, generosity, humility, forgiveness and refusing jealousy or grudges. Listeners are encouraged to put love into deeds within their local fellowship and to speak the gospel boldly, trusting God rather than themselves to give life through his word.
29976:
In 1 Peter 1:17–21, the preacher turns from the command to live reverently before God to the reason believers can do so: they have been redeemed. He begins with stories of homes, land and cars to show how readily people put prices on passing possessions. Peter contrasts such perishable things, including silver and gold, with the precious blood of Christ. The sermon presents redemption as being bought out of a futile former way of life, not purchased through wealth, good deeds or faithfulness. Because the price is Christ's own life, the preacher calls this rescue beyond any earthly valuation.

He then looks at the Redeemer himself. Christ is described as the spotless lamb whose coming was not an afterthought, who appeared for his people, died, was raised and received glory. In the preacher's reading, these truths anchor faith and hope in God and give persecuted believers assurance. The message asks listeners what they truly prize: if Christ's redemption is precious to them, it should move them towards holiness, gratitude, forgiveness and service rather than attachment to passing rewards. He urges families to pass on the news of Christ above material security, and invites those who do not know him to come rather than try to buy their way to God.
29977:
In this sermon on 1 Peter 2:1–3, the preacher calls believers to make room for God's Word and to desire it as urgently as a newborn desires milk. He first clarifies that Christ's saving work is complete: putting sin aside is a response of sanctification, not a way to earn justification. Using the picture of a healthier diet, he explains why malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy and slander must not be treated as harmless habits. Such attitudes damage relationships within the church and obstruct spiritual growth. He urges listeners to deal with them honestly, relying on God's power rather than excusing one form of sin while condemning another.

The sermon then turns to the positive command to long for the pure Word. The preacher uses family stories about infants needing milk to illustrate dependence, not merely a beginner's stage of faith. Scripture is to be sought because it leads believers to Christ and nourishes their growth in salvation. He warns against studying only to win arguments or collecting Bibles while neglecting to read them. Those who have tasted the Lord's kindness are encouraged to return to his Word with gratitude and desire. Unbelieving listeners are invited to come to Jesus and find life in him.
29981:
Returning from time away, the preacher expresses gratitude for his local church and asks what makes membership more than a name on a list. His central appeal is for meaningful participation that deepens love for Christ through committed life with his people. Drawing on Hebrews 3:13, he warns that sin deceives and hardens people when they remain isolated. Fellow believers can lovingly point out blind spots, urge repentance, and remind one another that Christ is better than the promises made by money, comfort or control. Membership gives this mutual encouragement a recognizable place in everyday life.

The preacher then surveys the Bible's commands to love, serve, forgive, encourage and bear one another's burdens. He argues that these commands call for real relationships within a local church, not merely warm feelings toward Christians elsewhere. Using the image of Christ's body, he asks whether members truly share one another's suffering and joy. Finally, he describes elders' responsibility to shepherd a known flock and members' responsibility to receive their care. Against a consumer approach to church, he urges listeners to make a clear, active commitment. He connects such unity and mutual support with perseverance in witness and a growing affection for Jesus and his church.
29982:
In this sermon on 1 Peter 2, the preacher uses the building of a house to explain why its foundation matters. He presents Jesus as the living, chosen and precious cornerstone of God's spiritual house. Without him, he says, the church cannot stand firm through the trials and persecution Peter addresses. Coming to Christ begins with repentance and faith, but the preacher also urges believers to keep drawing near to him for refuge, strength and fellowship. He asks listeners not to settle for outward religious activity while remaining apart from the one on whom the whole building depends.

The preacher then describes believers as living stones whom God is fitting together, rather than isolated bricks. Their shared life is meant to reflect their builder and to encourage one another amid suffering. Peter's image of a holy priesthood leads him to explain that Christ has opened access to God and that believers now offer spiritual sacrifices through him. He names the practical service of one's whole life, praise, doing good, sharing, witness and prayer. These are not substitutes for Christ's foundation, but ways of serving upon it. The sermon closes by urging gratitude, reverence and useful participation in the church, while inviting unbelieving listeners to rest on Christ rather than their own works.
29984:
Preaching from Luke 3:7–11, the speaker asks what genuine repentance looks like as John the Baptist prepares people for Jesus. He warns against treating baptism or other religious activities as a way to earn salvation. Nor can a family connection, even descent from Abraham or a godly home, transfer faith to another person. John's image of an axe already at the roots gives the appeal urgency: do not postpone turning from self-reliance to Christ. The preacher insists that Jesus alone is the refuge for sinners, while the fruit of repentance is evidence of new life rather than its purchase price.

The sermon then considers John's practical answer to people asking what they should do. Sharing an extra garment and food with someone in need illustrates fruit visible in ordinary life. The preacher is careful not to present generosity as another ladder to acceptance with God. Instead, he describes a person resting in Christ, whose kindness awakens a desire to reflect Christ's care for others. He challenges both those relying on religious performance and those delaying repentance to come to Jesus now. Believers are encouraged to trust him beyond the beginning of salvation and to show compassion, especially within the household of faith, in deed as well as words.
29992:
From Luke 3:14–16, the preacher contrasts John the Baptist with the far mightier Christ to whom John points. He first recalls John's answers to tax collectors and soldiers: genuine repentance should become visible in honesty, restraint and contentment rather than misuse of power. Yet neither these actions nor water baptism can cleanse the heart by themselves. When the crowds wonder whether John is the Messiah, John plainly refuses that place and directs their expectation beyond himself. The sermon asks listeners not to anchor their hope in even the most admired human leader.

The preacher then explores Christ's might and worth. John's statement that he is unworthy to untie the coming one's sandals becomes a call to humility and worship. John can baptize with water, but Jesus can baptize with the Holy Spirit; the preacher describes the Spirit's work in cleansing, strengthening and uniting believers. He also interprets baptism with fire as a warning of judgment, not an experience to seek. The sermon invites believers to return to Christ with renewed joy instead of being distracted by lesser things. Those who do not know him are urged to trust him rather than their background or works, and not to dismiss the seriousness of rejecting him.
29993:
First Peter 2 presents Jesus as the living cornerstone and divides humanity by its response to Him. Some examine His claims yet reject Him, stumbling over the One God has made the foundation. Others believe, find Him precious, and are built together as living stones. The sermon urges each hearer to ask who Jesus is to them personally. Respectful words about Him are not enough; salvation rests on trusting Christ rather than self-righteousness, religious effort, or any other foundation.

Peter then describes believers through remarkable Old Testament language. They are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and God’s own possession. These privileges do not arise from their worth, ethnicity, or achievements, but from God’s merciful love in Christ. They give Christians a shared identity that crosses ordinary national and cultural divisions. Yet this identity also carries a purpose: God’s people are left in the world to proclaim the excellencies of the One who called them out of darkness into His marvellous light. They display Christ both in their words and in lives set apart from the world. The sermon therefore calls believers to treasure Jesus, humbly remember the mercy they have received, and make their royal King known without fear, trusting God alone to give spiritual life.
30012:
John the Baptist’s picture in Luke 3:17 presents Jesus as the mighty farmer of salvation. Holding His winnowing fork, Christ owns the harvest and possesses final authority over every person. The threshing floor, tool, and barn are His, and no plan can resist His rule. His fork also reveals perfect discernment: Jesus sees hidden motives and distinguishes genuine disciples from empty profession. Nothing in the human heart is concealed from Him.

The farmer thoroughly clears the floor, showing Christ’s uncompromising purity. He will remove falsehood, hypocrisy, and sin, and His own holiness has power to cleanse what is defiled. Yet this mighty purity is joined to tender love. Jesus gathers the wheat—His redeemed people—carefully into the safety of His barn. He chose them, gave His life for them, awakens them, holds them securely, and promises to lose none. The same passage gives a solemn warning: the chaff, representing fruitless profession and unforgiven sin, is burned with unquenchable fire. Every sin must be answered either by Christ’s saving work on the cross or in final judgment. The sermon calls believers to find identity, security, and freedom from anxiety in the authoritative, discerning, pure, and loving Saviour. It urges those outside Christ not to underestimate Him, but to receive His freely offered grace while there is time.
30013:
From Luke 3:18–20, the preacher considers how John the Baptist's ministry embodied his witness to the mighty Christ. He presents three responses for those who embrace Jesus: proclaim him boldly, confront significant sin lovingly, and accept the cost of faithfulness. John's repeated preaching of the gospel is described as more than detached information. It included warning, pleading, urgency and comfort, as he called people to trust Christ rather than themselves. The preacher cautions against insisting that only one tone can communicate the gospel, while keeping the offer of Christ at the center.

John also rebuked Herod's public wrongdoing without favoritism. The preacher says such confrontation was not a claim that moral improvement saves; it exposed the need for Christ and protected people affected by corrupt leadership. Herod responded by imprisoning John. Listeners are urged not to harden themselves when corrected but to bring their sin to the Savior who can forgive and strengthen them. The preacher rejects the idea that John's shortened ministry was a failure measured by popularity or length. He argues that faithfulness is the better measure. Rather than copying John's exact calling, believers should speak of Christ and resist compromise wherever they have been placed, trusting him amid possible cost.
30019:
Opening a three-part study of Job under the theme "the sovereign Lord, the suffering saint and the devil's role", this sermon looks at Job 1:1-5 to present a Christian character worth imitating, because understanding Job's character is the key to understanding his suffering. God himself says there is none like Job on the earth: blameless and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil. Blameless does not mean sinless but growing in holiness, hating sin and putting it to death, with inner holiness visible in outward conduct. The sermon warns believers not to assume, as Job's friends did, that every suffering saint must be sinning, since God sometimes allows suffering for his own glory, as Jesus showed in John 9.

Job was also generous in heart. Though he was the greatest man in the East, his wealth did not lead him astray; he provided for his many servants and their families, and when everything was taken he still worshipped, saying, "The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away." He was spiritual in heart, rising early to offer sacrifices in case his children had sinned against God in their hearts. Fathers are urged to pray for their children and feed them spiritually rather than only providing material things, and believers to love and pray for their church family, so that they stand firm when trials come.
30020:
Job 1:13–22 confronts the question of worship when a comfortable day becomes a day of devastating loss. Beginning with Christ's suffering, the preacher turns to Job's successive disasters and his response, asking whether devotion depends only on received blessings.

Messengers report the loss of livestock, servants, and children before Job can process the earlier news. The sermon emphasizes the suddenness and severity of the suffering, while locating Satan's attack within God's sovereign permission rather than an uncontrolled world.

Job grieves and worships. Tearing his robe and shaving his head express anguish; falling before the Lord expresses continued allegiance. The preacher does not present worship as the absence of sorrow, but as honoring God amid it.

The Lord gives and takes away, and earthly possessions cannot be carried beyond life. Hearers are encouraged to receive loved ones and material gifts gratefully without making them the final basis of faith.

The application calls believers to trust God's purpose even when its details remain unseen. Christ's cross and Job's later confidence about emerging as gold supply grounds for hope in refinement. Unbelievers are urged not to postpone seeking mercy. The concluding prayer seeks humility, surrender, and comfort in the sovereign Lord rather than wasted opportunities to worship during trials.
30021:
Preaching from Luke 3:21–22, the speaker invites listeners to consider Jesus' baptism as the beginning of his public mission. He emphasizes the surprising humility of the sinless Son standing among people who came confessing sins. Jesus did not need repentance himself. The preacher gives two reasons for his baptism: he identifies with the people he came to save, and he undertakes the obedient life they could not live. He connects that obedience with Christ's righteousness as well as his bearing of sin, urging believers to approach God on Christ's merit rather than waiting until they feel worthy.

The sermon then follows the scene as Jesus prays, the Holy Spirit descends, and the Father speaks. The preacher describes Jesus in his human life as dependent on the Spirit and calls believers to rely on the Spirit too. He stresses that the Spirit's descent is described as being like a dove, not that the Spirit is literally a bird. The Father's words, calling Jesus his beloved Son and expressing pleasure in him, reveal a love that did not begin with this event. The speaker invites believers to delight in the Son whom the Father loves and offers unbelieving listeners a direct appeal to receive him. Throughout, his aim is to direct attention to Jesus' humility, dependence and belovedness.
30022:
The preacher approaches Luke 3:23–38, the genealogy of Jesus, as more than a difficult list of names. He says the family line places Jesus in real human history and invites listeners to see why he is the Savior they need. He organizes the sermon around five relationships in the list. As the supposed son of Joseph, Jesus entered ordinary human life while, in the preacher's account, Joseph was his legal rather than biological father. He connects this with Jesus' sinless life and his ability to act for sinners. As David's son, Jesus is presented as the promised king; as Abraham's son, the one through whom blessing reaches the nations.

Tracing the line further to Adam, the preacher contrasts the disobedience associated with the first man with Christ's obedience and his bearing of sin's curse. He then distinguishes Jesus' sonship of God from being a child of God by creation or adoption, proclaiming him divine. These are theological conclusions the preacher draws from the genealogy and related passages, not an invitation to guess at unknown names. He urges listeners to bring suffering and guilt to Christ, trust him as king and blessing giver, and worship him as the Son of God. The sermon closes by asking for deeper satisfaction in knowing Jesus.
30023:
Taking a break from Luke, the preacher begins a series on Christ-centered family life with Colossians 3:18 and its instruction to wives. He places the verse after Paul's call for Christ's word to dwell richly in the church and for every word and deed to be done in Jesus' name. In the preacher's account, a wife's voluntary submission to her own husband is a response to Christ's lordship, not a statement of lesser worth or an excuse for her husband to coerce her. He explicitly says she should think for herself, may enjoy Christ directly, and should not follow a direction contrary to God's Word.

The sermon connects marriage with the relationship between Christ and his church, drawing also on Ephesians 5. The preacher urges wives to seek satisfaction in Christ rather than trying to make a husband provide what only Christ can give. He asks them to express respect and gentleness in disagreements, support their husband's leadership and avoid continual contention. He also tells husbands that this command is addressed to wives, not an entitlement they may demand. His stated aim is a willing response flowing from devotion to Jesus, while acknowledging that living with an unreasonable husband can be difficult.
30024:
In this sermon on 1 Peter 2:11–12, the preacher urges believers to live as people whose ultimate home is not this world. Peter addresses them as beloved before calling them to abstain from desires that wage war against the soul. The preacher says awareness of God's love makes the instruction an appeal to grateful obedience, not a way to earn salvation. He warns that Christians can gradually become comfortable with attitudes and habits that draw them away from Christ. Because the old flesh still troubles believers, they must recognize the inward conflict and resist desires that weaken their joy and usefulness.

The sermon does not end with what to reject. Peter also calls for excellent conduct among outsiders, even when believers are misunderstood or slandered. The preacher describes this as a pattern of putting off harmful desires while putting on a life that reflects Jesus in speech, patience and action. He stresses dependence on Christ rather than mere self-improvement. He discusses two possible readings of the day of visitation and favors the hope that observers may glorify God when they see faithful conduct and hear the gospel. Listeners are encouraged to examine their choices, love fellow believers, endure unjust criticism for doing right and bear witness to Christ without blending unthinkingly into surrounding culture.
30033:
Beginning a series on discipleship, the preacher asks what a healthy follower of Jesus looks like. From Matthew 16:24, he argues that church programs, attendance and knowledge alone cannot define discipleship. Jesus speaks to those who are already his disciples, so denying oneself and carrying a cross are not fees that purchase forgiveness. The preacher first stresses the purpose of following: those saved by grace continue coming to Christ because they find rest, nourishment and joy in him. He contrasts that lasting satisfaction with a desire for an easy life that treats Jesus as a small addition to other pursuits.

The sermon then explores the three demands of the verse: deny oneself, take up one's cross and follow Jesus. Denying oneself means refusing self-rule rather than merely giving up a treat. Taking up the cross means willingness to bear shame, rejection or persecution for Christ, not simply naming every ordinary hardship a cross. Following him is an ongoing response that reaches everyday decisions, including work and leisure, without declaring those activities wrong in themselves. The preacher admits believers will stumble and calls them back to repentance and Christ's strength rather than pretending at instant perfection. He invites listeners to yield their lives willingly to the Savior who gave himself for them.
30034:
Continuing a series on discipleship, the preacher asks how believers grow in the costly life Jesus described as denying self, taking up the cross and following him. He first repeats that people become disciples by grace through faith in Christ, not by making themselves worthy. Growth, however, is not meant to be a private project. He argues that Christ has given the local church as the setting where disciples receive help and learn to serve. From Hebrews 3:13, he explains how sin can deceive and harden someone who remains isolated, and why believers need others who will lovingly identify blind spots and remind them of Christ's worth.

The preacher then turns to the call in 1 Thessalonians 5:11 to encourage and build one another up. When following Jesus brings weariness or opposition, fellow believers can offer more than distant reassurance: they can know a person's struggles and speak hope into them. Finally, Ephesians 4:11–16 pictures the body growing as each part works properly under Christ its head. The preacher urges members not merely to attend briefly but to open their lives, use their gifts and contribute to one another's maturity. His application is for believers to resist individualism and receive Christ's care through committed relationships in a local church.
30059:
At the beginning of a new year, the preacher turns to Psalm 13 for listeners carrying an unresolved question: how long? He says David's lament should keep believers from judging someone who feels down or distant from God. David repeatedly asks whether God has forgotten him, describes sorrow within and sees enemies rising against him. The preacher understands this as David's experience rather than proof that God has actually abandoned him. He cautions against allowing painful feelings to become the final measure of what is true, while acknowledging that the feelings and the prolonged trouble are real.

The sermon traces a movement from problem to prayer to praise. David asks God to consider him, answer him and enlighten his eyes. The preacher says prayer may change the sufferer's perspective even when the circumstance remains unresolved. David then remembers God's lovingkindness, rejoices in salvation and determines to sing because God has dealt generously with him. The preacher applies this by urging listeners to bring their ongoing troubles to God, remember Christ's saving love and trust his promise not to forsake them. He also invites those who do not yet know Christ to rest in what Jesus has done rather than wait for a particular feeling as proof that they may come to him.
30060:
In this part of the discipleship series, the sermon turns to Jesus’ commission in Matthew 28:18–20. Because Jesus has authority in heaven and on earth, making disciples is presented as a command for every follower, not a task reserved for pastors or overseas missionaries. The preacher describes three connected practices: share Christ with people wherever life takes you, share life with fellow believers in the local church, and share God’s word so that disciples learn to obey Jesus. Evangelism is the beginning, not the end, of this work.

Baptism is discussed as a public declaration of belonging to Christ and entering the church’s fellowship. Within that fellowship, believers encourage, serve, forgive, pray for, and bear with one another. The sermon gives particular weight to speaking biblical truth in love: hospitality and patience matter, but fellowship should also help people understand and practise Jesus’ commands. Teaching is more than transferring information; it includes modelling obedience, patient counsel, encouragement and correction. For those who feel too busy, inexperienced or unsure how to begin, the preacher suggests ordinary opportunities in family routines, conversations, prayer and shared reading. The invitation is to make disciples intentionally in everyday life, with Christ rather than personal ability at the centre.
30061:
Drawing on Colossians 1:28–29, this closing sermon in the discipleship series asks what gives believers the desire and endurance to make disciples. The preacher points repeatedly to Christ. Christ is the content of disciple-making: conversations, teaching and correction should direct people to him rather than to our achievements or interests. Christ is also its goal: the desire is to see people grow toward maturity in him. The sermon connects that desire with enjoying Christ oneself and sharing that joy with others.

The preacher then considers the cost of this work. Paul’s words about labouring and striving are presented as a call to sustained effort, including time spent teaching, seeking out struggling believers and bearing hardship. Yet the sermon does not present determination alone as sufficient. Paul strives according to Christ’s power at work in him, and the preacher urges listeners to rely on that strength while remembering Christ’s worth. Those who feel little motivation are invited to look again at the one they proclaim, the people they hope to help mature, and the strength he supplies. Disciple-making is framed not as an optional extra to worship, but as a way of honouring Christ in everyday service.
30062:
Romans 1:14–18 displays Paul’s readiness to proclaim the precious gospel without shame. He feels an obligation to Greeks and non-Greeks, to the wise and the foolish, because the good news is for every kind of person. Paul does not choose hearers by appearance, background, or social standing. Even persecution, ridicule, prison, and death cannot silence him, for speaking about Jesus is an honour and lost people need the one message that can save them.
