Paul gives the reason for this confidence: the gospel is God’s power for salvation to everyone who believes. Human eloquence, religious effort, and moral deeds cannot give spiritual life. God works through the message of Christ crucified and risen to bring dead sinners to life. Those who trust Jesus receive a righteousness that is not their own—the perfect righteousness of Christ credited to them. This salvation begins and continues by faith, and genuine faith becomes visible in a changed life and an unashamed witness. The urgency is sharpened by the reality of God’s wrath against sin, but Christians proclaim good news rather than condemnation alone: Christ has borne judgment for those who believe. The sermon calls believers to examine their fear, refuse selective evangelism, and lovingly tell friends, family, neighbours, and strangers that salvation is found in Jesus alone.
30063:
Hebrews 11:1–3 explains how Christians persevere through trials by faith. Biblical faith is not wishful thinking, positive feeling, or a power people generate to obtain what they want. Saving faith includes true knowledge of God’s revelation, agreement that it is true, and personal trust in God and His Word. Salvation is entirely by grace, so faith renounces self-sufficiency and rests in Christ. That trust is active: it produces a changed life and continues to govern the believer long after conversion.

Faith gives present substance to God’s future promises and settled conviction about realities that cannot yet be seen. Resurrection, final justice, eternal rest, Christ’s intercession, and the unshakable kingdom become weighty enough to shape choices now. This enables Christians to forgive rather than retaliate, worship through pain, give generously, and pursue what will endure. God commends this life of trust, whether it appears extraordinary or ordinary and whether faith leads to deliverance or costly suffering. The Old Testament believers in Hebrews were flawed people in varied circumstances, but they relied on God. Faith also recognises God and His Word as the ultimate reality behind creation. The sermon therefore calls Christians to stop measuring God’s favour by comfort or visible results and to persevere by resting even weak faith in the strong and faithful Saviour.
30064:
Jesus’ parable of the rich fool exposes the danger of believing that life is secured by possessions. When a man interrupts Jesus over an inheritance dispute, Jesus identifies the deeper problem: covetousness. The prosperous farmer in the parable receives an abundant harvest, but treats every gift as his own. He plans larger barns and a life of ease while forgetting God, his neighbour, the true purpose of life, and the certainty of eternity. His sudden death reveals how foolish it is to build a future around wealth while neglecting the soul.

The sermon calls listeners to guard their hearts because possessions can begin to possess the people who own them. Being rich toward God is not determined by salary, nor does it make saving, holidays, or wealth inherently wrong. It means receiving God’s gifts as a steward and using time, talents, and treasure for God’s interests and the good of others. This self-denying generosity grows from the gospel: Jesus Christ became poor for sinners so that they might receive forgiveness, eternal life, adoption, and an unfading inheritance. Those who believe this good news are freed from living for themselves and invited to serve God and neighbour with what they have been given.
30066:
In the first of two messages on gossip, the preacher turns to Proverbs 6:12–19 and other passages to urge the church to protect its unity. He begins by giving thanks for the congregation’s care for one another, then warns that malicious speech can damage the fellowship it values. He describes gossip and slander as the sharing of harmful reports with a motive to lower another person’s reputation. His concern is not limited to false claims: even a true detail can be passed on destructively.

The sermon traces the harm in three directions. Gossip damages the speaker, drawing them toward strife and costing the trust of others. It damages listeners, who may become suspicious of a brother or sister and quietly withdraw. It also wounds the person discussed, who may not know what has been said or have a fair chance to respond. The preacher notes that harmful reports can arrive disguised as a request for sympathy or prayer, so the hearer should not passively encourage them. He ends by pointing to Christ’s care for his people and calling believers to protect one another’s honour. Practical steps for responding to gossip are promised for the following message rather than fully developed here.
30068:
Following an earlier warning about the damage gossip can cause, this sermon turns to Proverbs 26:20–22 to ask how a church can respond. The preacher gives three memorable instructions: do not transmit a harmful report, do not receive it eagerly, and step away from a persistent pattern of divisive speech. As wood feeds a fire, repeating a rumour can prolong conflict; refusing to pass it on can help contention quiet down. He also observes that gossip may feel attractive to the hearer because of self-righteousness, a desire for control or a desire to be accepted.

The sermon makes room for important distinctions. Not every discussion of a difficult matter is gossip: someone directly involved in a serious problem or invited to help resolve it may need to speak and listen. Leaders, in particular, are urged not to assume an allegation is established simply because one person speaks first. The preacher says a genuine request for help should be heard with care, while also protecting the person accused from an unverified judgement. He includes the possibility of seeking appropriate authority in a severe situation. Throughout, he points listeners toward Christ’s care for his people as their reason to guard one another’s reputations and pursue truthful, loving fellowship.
30069:
Peter’s instruction in 1 Peter 2:13–17 calls Christians to submit to earthly authorities for the Lord’s sake. God establishes spheres of authority to promote order, restrain wrongdoing, and serve human good. Although governing leaders may be unjust or personally disagreeable, believers are normally to live as respectful, law-abiding citizens. Their submission is ultimately offered to Christ, whose authority stands above every earthly ruler and whose patient endurance provides their example.

The sermon gives four reasons for this obedience: it honours the Lord, recognises that authority exists under God’s sovereignty, fulfils God’s will by silencing false accusations through good conduct, and uses Christian freedom in the service of God rather than as a cover for rebellion. Peter’s summary—honour all people, love the brotherhood, fear God, and honour the king—keeps civil conduct within a larger life of worship and love. This command does have a clear limit. When any authority requires disobedience to God, Christians must obey God rather than people, while remaining faithful witnesses to Christ. The sermon therefore urges believers to pray for leaders, resist being consumed by political conflict, pursue peace, and give their primary energy to the gospel and the kingdom of God.
30070:
Using 1 John 2:15–17, this sermon asks believers to examine the direction of their love. The preacher contrasts God’s love shown in Christ and the love believers should show one another with the forbidden love of “the world.” He explains that this does not mean despising creation, other people or the ordinary gifts of a holiday or home. His concern is a pattern of desires that takes those gifts and makes them rivals to Christ. John’s categories of the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes and the pride of life provide the framework for that examination.

The sermon asks listeners what they crave, pursue and boast about. Possessions, pleasure, status and recognition can become consuming when they displace love for Jesus and care for his people. The preacher warns that a settled allegiance to such desires is incompatible with the love of the Father, while acknowledging that believers can be tempted and need to return to Christ. The world and its desires are passing away, whereas John points to the one who does God’s will as abiding forever. Rather than treating created things as the final treasure, listeners are invited to enjoy them with gratitude, seek God’s word and presence, and set their hearts on Christ.
30071:
This first message on Jesus in the Nazareth synagogue opens the narrative of Luke 4:14–30 but concentrates on verses 14–21. The preacher follows Jesus as he returns to Galilee in the Spirit’s power and teaches in synagogues, then reads from Isaiah in the place where he grew up. He emphasizes that teaching God’s word is central to Jesus’ ministry. The initially favourable response to Jesus is not treated as the same thing as trusting him; the preacher asks listeners whether their admiration becomes genuine devotion.

Jesus reads a promise of good news to the poor, release for captives, sight for the blind and freedom for the oppressed, then announces that the Scripture is fulfilled in their hearing. The sermon interprets these images as a picture of human spiritual need and of the rescue Jesus offers. The poor cannot provide their own righteousness, captives need release, the blind need sight, and the oppressed need relief. The announced favourable year is presented as a time of forgiveness and freedom. Listeners are invited to recognise their need and turn to Christ rather than merely observe the scene from a distance. Believers are encouraged that Jesus came for needy people and urged to remain humble, since their dependence on him does not end when they first believe.
30073:
In 1 Peter 2:18–21, the preacher considers how Christians respond when they are treated unfairly. Peter addresses servants under masters, including unreasonable ones, and commends patient endurance when someone suffers for doing what is right. The sermon draws a broader application to workplaces and other relationships, asking how a believer can act with respect and grace even when another person is harsh. The preacher repeatedly distinguishes this from endorsing slavery or excusing mistreatment. His focus is the believer’s response while facing it, not a claim that unjust treatment is good.

The sermon looks to Christ as the example of one who suffered without retaliating and calls listeners to serve him in their conduct toward others. Joseph’s response to his brothers is used as another picture of showing grace without calling their evil actions acceptable. The preacher says God’s grace, a conscience directed toward him and the promise that he sees patient endurance can sustain such a response. Doing wrong and bearing its consequences is distinguished from doing right and suffering unjustly. The workplace illustration ends with an explicit qualification: a person does not have to remain under a mistreating boss and may leave. Listeners are invited to examine their first reaction to unfairness and seek a God-honouring response without denying the wrong done.
30074:
Luke 4:1–13 recounts Jesus’ temptation in the wilderness. The preacher says the passage is first an invitation to behold Jesus as the faithful Son and representative, rather than merely a set of tactics for resisting temptation. After forty days without food, Jesus faces the devil’s offers at a point of real human weakness. Where Adam and Israel failed, the sermon presents Jesus as unwavering in his trust, worship and obedience. His responses from Scripture reveal the heart of each temptation, not just a convenient quotation to defeat an argument.

The first offer, turning stone to bread, is interpreted as a challenge to trust the Father’s care amid hunger. The offer of worldly kingdoms without the path of suffering presses Jesus to value a shortcut above worship of God alone. At the temple, a promise of angelic protection is used out of context to urge reckless self-direction. Jesus refuses to make God serve his own plans. The preacher invites listeners to admire the one who endured these pressures without yielding, and to find encouragement rather than despair when they recognise their own failures. Drawing on Hebrews, he urges those who struggle to approach Christ for mercy and help, trusting that this sympathetic high priest understands temptation and supplies grace in need.
30075:
Returning to Jesus’ visit to the Nazareth synagogue, this message concentrates on Luke 4:22–30. The people initially marvel at his gracious words, but their response changes when they measure his claim against their familiarity with his family and demand signs in his hometown. The preacher sees three related barriers to receiving Jesus: familiarity that becomes presumption, self-righteousness that cannot acknowledge need, and a diminished view of his power. Being near biblical teaching, he warns, is not the same as trusting the person to whom it points.

Jesus recalls two outsiders who received help in the days of Elijah and Elisha: a widow in need during famine and Naaman seeking cleansing. The sermon contrasts their need and eventual trust with the hometown audience’s sense of entitlement. When Jesus challenges that audience, admiration turns to anger and they try to drive him out. Listeners are urged not to repeat that movement by treating religious knowledge as a substitute for meeting Christ, defending their own righteousness, or assuming he is too small to help them. The preacher calls both believers and those who do not yet trust Jesus to admit their need and come to him. For believers, the response includes humility, continued faith and an openness to correction that leads them back to Christ.
30076:
Colossians 1:14 gives believers three reasons for lasting gratitude: union with Christ, redemption through Christ, and forgiveness because of Christ. Against the pressure of trials and discouragement, the message invites listeners to dwell on these spiritual blessings. Its central application is to cultivate thankfulness by remembering what God has already given, rather than allowing present difficulties to define the whole of life.

The words 'in whom' introduce the believer's intimate relationship with Jesus. Images of a building and foundation, branches and vine, body and head, and bride and bridegroom illustrate dependence, care and security. The preacher traces this union through salvation and explains redemption as release from slavery at a costly ransom. Christ's blood, not material wealth, provides the price, bringing freedom from sin's mastery and its penalty.

Forgiveness is presented as embracing all the believer's sins, with the removal of condemnation supplying grounds for assurance and joy. This confidence is not an invitation to continue pursuing sin: listeners are encouraged to resist temptation and find their satisfaction in Christ. Believers are urged to meditate on these gifts, speak about them with one another, and respond with gratitude through suffering. Those who have not trusted Christ are invited to turn from sin and come to him in faith.
30077:
Who is Jesus Christ, and how should knowing him shape everyday life? In Colossians 1:15, the preacher follows two descriptions of Jesus: the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of all creation. The message moves from thanksgiving for what Christ has done to praise for who he is, calling listeners to give him honour at home, at work and in church.

The first description is explained as much more than an outward resemblance. Jesus shares the divine nature and perfectly reveals God's glory. The preacher carefully distinguishes the Son from the Father while affirming their unity, and argues that Christ did not become divine when he took human flesh. His identity is eternal, not the status of a created angel or merely a human messenger.

The second description concerns supremacy rather than a beginning in time. Biblical examples of firstborn status illustrate inheritance, authority and rank. The following verse's account of Christ creating all things supports his right to rule over creation. These truths lead to a personal challenge: recognising Christ's identity must become wholehearted allegiance. Listeners are invited to trust him for salvation rather than their own goodness, give him their hearts, and make knowing him their highest pursuit.
30078:
Luke 4:31–37 presents Jesus teaching in the synagogue and commanding an unclean spirit to leave a man. The message contrasts this encounter with the rejection of Jesus in Nazareth, challenging a familiarity with religious things that leaves self-righteousness untouched. Listeners are invited to recognise Christ's authority rather than reduce him to a manageable figure who makes little difference to their lives.

Jesus' teaching is explored through its divine origin, significant content, clear illustrations, compassionate purpose and direct address to the heart. His words do more than regulate outward behaviour: they engage the mind, expose motives and call people to himself. The preacher therefore emphasises the central place of God's word in the church's life and ministry.

The confrontation with the demon makes the same authority visible in action. Jesus silences the spirit and commands its departure without a struggle between equal powers. The man is released without harm, and the witnesses connect the miracle with the authority of Jesus' message. Their amazement spreads news throughout the surrounding region.

The final appeal goes beyond admiration. Christ's holiness and power are presented as reasons for sinners to seek his saving mercy, not flee from him. Believers are called to abandon self-righteousness, exalt Christ in their hearts and respond to him with faith.
30079:
In Luke 4:38–41, Jesus' authority is revealed through personal compassion. The message follows three scenes: the healing of Simon's mother-in-law, the crowds bringing their sick to Jesus, and his commands to the demons. Together they present a Saviour who draws near to vulnerable people and whose power is sufficient for their needs. This view of Christ challenges the self-righteousness discussed in the preceding passages.

The first healing joins tenderness with effective authority. Jesus attends to the woman, the fever leaves, and she immediately rises to serve. As more people arrive, he lays his hands on each one. The preacher emphasises this individual attention rather than treating the crowd as an anonymous burden. His care is not separated from his power, and his authority is not presented as cold or distant.

The demons also obey him, but Jesus refuses to let them speak on his behalf. The message connects these displays of authority with his messianic mission and ultimately his victory through the cross and resurrection.

Listeners who suffer are encouraged to bring their pain to Christ and seek their deepest comfort in him. The preacher expressly distinguishes this invitation from a promise of immediate physical recovery. The closing call is to trust his compassion, cling to him and dedicate life to him.
30080:
First Peter 2 presents Christ as the model and hope for Christians who suffer unjustly. Believers should not be surprised by mistreatment, because Jesus warned that his followers would face persecution. Peter directs them to the sinless Christ, who endured the cross without reviling his attackers or threatening revenge. Instead, Jesus entrusted himself to the Father who judges righteously. His response was not weakness or passivity; he was fulfilling the Father’s will and redeeming his people. Christ bore their sins so that they could die to sin, live to righteousness, and return to the shepherd and guardian of their souls.

The sermon calls Christians to trace the pattern of Jesus’ life. When insulted or treated unfairly, they should resist retaliation, speak truth with kindness, entrust justice to God and remember that they needed mercy. Following Christ does not mean reproducing his atoning work, nor does it require perfect strength. The Holy Spirit helps believers walk in the footsteps of their shepherd, whose presence is near in suffering. Remembering and preaching the gospel to themselves warms the heart and gives strength for humble obedience. By looking to the cross, Christians can forgive, put sin to death, live faithfully and even rejoice that they have been counted worthy to suffer for Jesus’ name.
30081:
Luke 4:42–44 shows Jesus remaining faithful to his mission when a grateful crowd wants him to stay. Following the preceding healings, the message considers his prayer, the pressure placed upon him, and his purpose in preaching the kingdom of God. The central challenge is to admire Christ's determination and then make his concern for the lost a priority in everyday life.

Jesus withdraws to a secluded place, with the parallel account identifying prayer as his purpose. The preacher presents this dependence on the Father as a pattern for those who would speak to others about God. Communion with God is not treated as an optional extra to public ministry, but as the place of rest and strength from which it proceeds.

The crowd's pursuit of Jesus raises a searching question about motives. Wanting his benefits is distinguished from receiving him as Saviour. Jesus does not allow popularity or the demand for further miracles to displace the purpose for which he was sent.

The good news offers salvation through Christ rather than earned acceptance. Those who receive him are urged to embrace his mission out of gratitude, not to win God's favour. The closing appeal encourages prayerful, compassionate gospel witness among family, neighbours, colleagues and others, even when fear or comfort makes silence easier.
30094:
What gives a Christian life its lasting purpose? Returning to Jesus’ resolve to preach the kingdom in Luke 4:43, this sermon challenges the assumption that comfort, possessions and an easy retirement are enough. Those who have received Christ’s mercy are called to make his excellencies known. Evangelism is presented as part of following Jesus, not merely an activity reserved for the pastor.

The preacher develops three motives for speaking about Christ: the horror of hell, the joy of heaven and the excellency of Christ himself. The seriousness of judgement calls for loving urgency towards people who do not know the gospel. Confidence in God’s sovereignty is not presented as a reason for indifference. Hope in the coming life also changes present priorities, while the sermon distinguishes freely received salvation from the rewards of faithful service.

The final emphasis is on knowing and enjoying Christ. Remembering his sacrifice, present care and enduring love can loosen the grip of self-protection and awaken a desire for others to know him. Listeners are urged to examine what occupies their hopes, prayers and conversations, and to pursue a lasting gospel purpose within their families and wider community.
30095:
Why would fishermen leave a remarkable catch behind to follow Jesus? This sermon explores Luke 5:1–11 as an encounter with someone more valuable than the security of an ordinary livelihood. Jesus draws Simon Peter and his companions into his mission by revealing his teaching, sovereignty, holiness, grace and calling. Their response grows from seeing who he is, not simply from being pressured to do more.

The preacher follows Simon from the distraction of washing nets to listening closely as Jesus teaches from his boat. An unsuccessful night of fishing then becomes the setting for an overwhelming catch at Jesus’ command. Peter sees more than an unexpected success: confronted by the Lord’s holiness, he recognises his own sinfulness. Jesus answers his fear with grace and calls him into a new purpose, catching people through the gospel.

Listeners are encouraged to attend to Christ’s word, trust his authority and confess their need of grace. The sermon expressly rejects using grace as an excuse to continue in sin. It also distinguishes the disciples’ particular departure from their occupations from the principle that applies to every believer: Christ deserves first place. Following him means relinquishing self-centred priorities and sharing his concern for people who need the gospel.
30096:
Jesus’ words to Simon Peter in Luke 5:10 form the centre of this sermon: do not fear, from now on, you will be catching people. After recalling the extraordinary catch of fish and Peter’s awareness of his sin, the preacher considers how Christ’s grace both receives a sinner and changes the direction of his life. Grace is not presented as acceptance that leaves a person unchanged.

The first emphasis is reassurance. Jesus already knows Peter’s weakness, deliberately comes near, offers healing and has the power to save. Recognising sin need not therefore lead Peter to retreat from the very Saviour he needs. The phrase “from now on” highlights Christ’s initiative at a moment of exposed unworthiness, rather than after Peter has made himself fit for service.

The promise of catching people is then explored as inward transformation, not merely outward conformity. Gospel work involves patient labour, rejection and discouragement, yet sharing in Christ’s purpose is a gracious privilege. The sermon points to Peter’s later perseverance as evidence of that change. Listeners are invited to slow down and consider Christ’s grace until gratitude and delight increasingly shape their motives for speaking about him, rather than relying on duty alone.
30097:
This sermon considers the Christian home as a place where faith must become visible in everyday conduct. Focusing on wives in 1 Peter 3:1–6, the preacher connects Peter’s instructions with the letter’s earlier teaching about hope, holiness and Christ’s example under suffering. Church activity, he argues, must not become a reason to overlook relationships at home.

The message explains submission to one’s own husband as part of honouring Christ, including where husband and wife do not share the same faith. It expressly says that a wife must not comply with a demand to sin, and warns husbands against using the passage as a weapon against their wives. The preacher also discusses the situation in which an unbelieving spouse chooses to leave.

Attention then turns to the character of this witness: respectful conduct, inward beauty, gentleness and a quiet spirit. These are contrasted with reliance on appearance or repeated arguments, not with a blanket prohibition on attractive clothing or speaking the gospel. Sarah and the women who hoped in God provide the closing example. Listeners are urged to look to Christ, pray for their husbands and seek a transformed heart. The sermon acknowledges that faithful conduct does not guarantee a spouse’s conversion.
30098:
When the fishermen leave everything and follow Jesus in Luke 5:11, what does their response reveal? This sermon directs attention away from admiration of their sacrifice and towards the worth of Christ. The preacher describes their decision as gaining a greater treasure, not simply exchanging security for an empty or miserable life. Seeing Christ’s glory is presented as the starting point for wholehearted devotion.

Three themes shape the exposition: deliberate obedience, Christ as the supreme treasure and wholehearted following. The return to shore is considered as an opportunity for reflection on Jesus’ sovereignty, holiness, mercy and gracious calling. The preacher distinguishes this deeper devotion from earning salvation, insisting that Christ alone saves and that leaving possessions or performing good works cannot remove sin.

The application is not a universal instruction to abandon employment or family responsibilities. Instead, listeners are asked whether their possessions and ambitions have come to possess them. Following Christ involves trusting him, submitting to his direction and treasuring him above competing loyalties. Work, family, resources and rest are to serve that central pursuit. The closing appeal encourages believers to help one another relinquish controlling attachments and consider the present joy of knowing Christ, alongside the lasting generosity of his promises.
30099:
A man covered with leprosy comes to Jesus with a simple appeal: if Jesus is willing, he can make him clean. Exploring this encounter in Luke 5, the sermon presents the healing as an illustration of salvation. Its three movements consider the ugliness of sin, the sinner’s plea and the Saviour’s response. The aim is to awaken gratitude for grace and a desire to tell others about Christ.

The preacher uses the man’s uncleanness and exclusion to illustrate the helplessness and separation associated with sin. The man approaches without credentials or a claim to deserve healing, yet with confidence in Jesus’ power. His request for cleansing is understood as pointing beyond outward relief towards restored fellowship with God.

Jesus’ touch and willing response receive particular attention. The sermon distinguishes believing that Christ has power from trusting his compassion towards the undeserving. Listeners troubled by repeated failures are directed to his welcome and to the cross as evidence of his mercy. The immediate cleansing then displays his authority. Finally, the instruction to appear before the priest shows respect for the law and makes the restored man a testimony to Jesus’ identity. Believers are encouraged to remember their own dependence on grace and speak of the Saviour who received them.
30107:
What does a Christ-centred husband look like behind closed doors? This sermon on 1 Peter 3:7 challenges the idea that leadership means demanding service, asserting superiority or withdrawing into private interests. The preacher places marriage under Christ’s example: the one who loved his church and gave himself for her. A husband’s conduct at home is presented as part of his witness, not a private exception to Christian discipleship.

The verse is developed through understanding, cherishing and honouring one’s wife. Understanding requires time, attentive listening and genuine knowledge of her concerns, strengths and fears. Shared residence or participation in church life cannot replace personal involvement. Care is to be patient and tender, not aggressive, controlling or dismissive. The sermon also stresses a wife’s dignity as a fellow heir of grace, while maintaining the duty of loving treatment where a spouse is not a believer.

The warning about hindered prayers connects daily conduct with spiritual fellowship. Husbands are urged to pray with and for their wives, examine distractions and show respect in both private and public speech. Young men are encouraged to develop these habits before marriage. The closing invitation turns to Christ as the bridegroom and calls those who do not know him to trust his finished work.
30108:
How can believers resist becoming absorbed in comfort and temporary pursuits? Beginning with Exodus 34:14, this sermon explores God’s jealousy as a motive for wholehearted devotion. The preacher distinguishes it from insecure, possessive human jealousy and describes it as an intense commitment to an exclusive relationship. The message asks listeners to consider not only what they avoid, but what their hearts actively pursue.

Three aspects guide the sermon: God’s jealousy for his glory, for his Son and for his people. His glory is presented as displayed through Christ, not in competition with him. The preacher connects the uniqueness of salvation in Jesus with the Father’s purpose to honour the Son. In addressing believers, he distinguishes God’s unchanging jealousy from condemnation, emphasising Christ’s bearing of wrath on behalf of the redeemed.

The final section considers the privileges and responsibilities of belonging to God. His love, faithfulness and devotion call forth grateful love and faithfulness in return. This response is not presented as earning salvation or claiming present sinless perfection. Listeners are urged to confess rival attachments, follow Christ and move beyond minimum compliance. A searching practical question closes the message: does a chosen pursuit help deepen love for Christ, or draw the heart away from him?
30109:
A crowded house becomes the setting for an extraordinary declaration: Jesus tells a paralysed man that his sins are forgiven. This sermon on Luke 5:15–20 follows the scene through the critics, the carriers and Christ. Before entering the house, it notices Jesus withdrawing to pray even as his popularity grows, modelling dependence on the Father rather than the approval of a crowd.

The religious critics provide a warning about approaching God’s word with self-satisfaction instead of need. The men carrying their helpless companion display a contrasting posture. When the crowd blocks their way, they bring him through the roof, determined to place him before Jesus. The preacher sees sacrificial love and confidence in Christ expressed through their persistence, and asks whether listeners discourage such service or willingly share its cost.

Jesus addresses the man’s deepest need with forgiveness. The sermon emphasises the compassion, grace and completeness of his response: he welcomes the needy person rather than demanding that he first establish his worthiness. The closing application calls believers to put aside self-righteousness, come to Christ honestly and help others approach him. This includes both people who need to hear the gospel and fellow believers weighed down by guilt or discouragement. The remainder of the narrative is reserved for a later message.
30115:
Who is Jesus, and why does the answer matter for forgiveness? Continuing the account of the paralysed man in Luke 5:21–26, this sermon examines Jesus’ authority as it is challenged, defended and publicly demonstrated. The religious leaders correctly recognise that forgiveness belongs to God, but their settled view of Jesus leads them to charge him with blasphemy rather than reconsider who stands before them.

The preacher warns that self-righteousness can make a person knowledgeable about Scripture while resistant to correction and unaware of personal need. Jesus then answers reasoning that has remained hidden in his opponents’ hearts. His question about forgiving sins and commanding a man to walk leads to a visible demonstration supporting his declaration of pardon. The title Son of Man is connected with the authority and kingdom described in Daniel.

The man rises, carries his stretcher home and glorifies God. The crowd’s astonishment matters, but the sermon distinguishes amazement from genuine trust in Christ. Listeners are asked to see more than a striking healing: the narrative reveals the one who knows hearts and has authority to forgive. The response urged is worship, grateful dependence and a life submitted to his word, including bringing self-righteousness itself before him rather than defending it.
30116:
First Peter describes the blessed life very differently from promises of success, comfort, or fulfilled personal ambition. Peter writes to persecuted believers and teaches that good days are possible even when outward circumstances remain hard. This life begins in the heart and is expressed within the church through harmony, sympathy, brotherly love, kindness, and humility. Christians are united not by identical preferences but by Jesus Christ and the essential truths of the gospel. His compassion, love, service, and humility become the pattern for relationships in which believers seek another person’s good without demanding anything in return.

The blessed life also changes how Christians respond to hostility. Instead of repaying evil, insult, or slander in kind, they turn from evil, do good, bless those who wrong them, and actively pursue peace. This is not permission to ignore sin, but a call to extend the grace and forgiveness believers have received from Christ. God’s caring eyes are toward the righteous and his ears attend to their prayers, while his face opposes persistent evil. The sermon asks listeners to examine where they seek fulfilment and whether hidden sin, resentment, pride, or self-interest is obstructing Christlike life together. Those who do not know Christ are directed first to trust him, because these virtues cannot earn salvation; they grow from his saving grace.
30118: This sermon opens Luke 5:27–32 by asking who receives the forgiveness Jesus has authority to give. It follows Jesus as he calls Levi, a despised tax collector, to leave his booth and follow him. Levi’s response and banquet show the reach of Christ’s grace toward people whom others regard as beyond repentance. The sermon contrasts that welcome with the grumbling and self-righteousness of the Pharisees and scribes, who see themselves as spiritually healthy and therefore fail to recognise their own need. Jesus’ picture of a physician explains that he came to call sinners to repentance: those who admit their sickness seek the doctor, while those who insist they are well exclude themselves. Listeners are encouraged not to hide behind pride, reputation, or comparisons with others, but to examine their sin honestly, bring it to Christ, and depend on him continually. The message is both an invitation and a warning: no sinner is outside the reach of Jesus’ call, yet self-righteousness can keep a person from receiving the grace, forgiveness, healing, and transforming fellowship that only Christ provides. It also challenges believers to resist standing apart from people in need and to remember that daily Christian life remains dependent on the same gracious physician.
30119:
Preaching on Luke 6:1-5, where the disciples pick and eat grain on the Sabbath, this sermon exposes legalism: piling man-made rules on top of God's commands until no one can breathe beneath them. Self-righteous people love legalism because it lets them polish their own goodness and condemn others. First, legalism condemns. What the disciples did was permitted by Deuteronomy 23:25, yet the Pharisees, acting as self-appointed referees, accused them of breaking their own rules. Their traditions had turned the Sabbath, God's gift of rest and delight, into a burden, like fences built around a garden until no one can enjoy it. Believers are warned not to confuse their own interpretation of God's law with God's law itself.

Second, Jesus defends. He answers from Scripture, pointing to David eating the consecrated bread: if God in compassion set aside his own ritual for the hungry, how much less should man-made rules bind anyone? Legalism is empty of compassion, because only those who see their own sin cling to Christ's mercy and learn to share it. Third, Jesus rules. As the Son of Man and Lord of the Sabbath, greater than the temple, he owns the day and declares it a day of mercy. He is Lord over our time, rest, money and convictions, so believers are urged to own their sin and replace condemnation with compassion.
30120:
Concluding a series on Jesus' five conflicts with the scribes and Pharisees in Luke, this sermon studies the healing of the man with the withered right hand in Luke 6:6-11. Since Genesis 3:15 the seed of the serpent has fought the seed of the woman, and here self-righteousness meets grace head on. First, the merciful Jesus rules by compassion. The Sabbath was meant to display God's mercy, yet the religious leaders watched Jesus closely, certain of his power and compassion, waiting to accuse him. Knowing their thoughts, Jesus boldly called the man to stand in the middle of the synagogue, refusing to withhold good from the suffering just to avoid offending the self-righteous.

Second, the merciful Jesus exposes self-righteousness. His question, whether it is lawful to do good or harm on the Sabbath, revealed men who examined others' withered hands while blind to their own withered hearts. Their silence grieved and angered him, and across the five conflicts their hearts hardened from questioning, to grumbling, to accusation, to plotting murder. Third, the merciful Jesus does good while his enemies rage: at his word the hand was restored, yet they left filled with fury. Listeners are warned that a decent religious life can still grieve Christ if it refuses correction, and are urged to ask God to burn out their self-righteousness and change them.
30121:
Beginning a new series on the twelve apostles from Luke 6:12-16, this sermon speaks to believers who see their weaknesses clearly and wonder how God could ever use them. God loves to accomplish the impossible through the weak, as Christ's own life shows: he died rejected and poor, yet he is the centre of all history. Before turning to the apostles, Luke fixes our eyes on Jesus as the real secret behind their accomplishment. First, Jesus is mighty in prayer. As hostility rose against him, he did not worry or escape but spent the whole night with his Father, depending on him for the choice of the Twelve and interceding for men who could not even stay awake to pray. He still intercedes for his people today.

Second, Jesus is mighty in choosing. From a great multitude of disciples he sovereignly called just twelve. As with Gideon's three hundred, God uses few so that the glory is plainly his. Third, Jesus is mighty in sending. Apostles are sent out to preach, and that purpose passes to the church. The list itself is striking: no scholars or generals, but fishermen, a zealot, a tax collector and a future traitor. The future of the gospel never rested on these men but on Christ's power, and with Paul believers can boast in their weaknesses.
30124:
Continuing in 1 Peter, this sermon works through 3:13-16, where Peter teaches believers how to respond to persecution and to the trials of life. "Who is there to harm you?" echoes Psalm 34: the Lord does not remove every affliction, but he is near the brokenhearted, and nothing touches his people unless he wills it. As Joseph's story and the cross show, God is sovereign even over the evil intentions of men. Those who suffer for righteousness are blessed, while suffering for doing wrong brings discipline, not reward. In hardship Satan whispers that God has abandoned us, so believers must stand on the written Word rather than their feelings, refusing to fear intimidation.

Instead of fearing, Christians are to sanctify Christ as Lord in their hearts, setting him apart through his Word, surrendering every circumstance to his lordship and drawing strength from him. From that place they must always be ready to defend the hope within them. The sermon corrects the idea that believers should speak only when asked: Peter's readers were questioned because they were already proclaiming Christ and living it. This defence is not for a few online debaters but for the whole church, and it must be made with gentleness, reverence and a clear conscience, aiming to win souls rather than arguments. Unbelievers are urged to trust Christ.
30125:
Introducing a new series on the twelve apostles from Luke 6:13, this sermon removes the marble-statue image of the apostles as superhuman saints. Like Elijah, they were men with a nature like ours. As a group they suffered from "big head disease", arguing over who was greatest even as Jesus spoke of his death. They had "turtle disease", repeatedly failing to understand his plain teaching, and "chicken disease", panicking in the storm and fleeing at his arrest. They were also controlling, turning away children and rebuking a man who cast out demons in Jesus' name. Yet Christ never gave up on them. He washed their feet, patiently taught and corrected them, calmed their fears and met them after the resurrection with "Peace be to you."

Through Christ, these ordinary men carried the gospel across the world, planted churches, wrote Scripture and joyfully suffered martyrdom. God delights to use the weak and despised (2 Corinthians 12:9; 1 Corinthians 1:26-28), so weakness is no barrier to being used by him. What set the apostles apart, Judas excepted, was that they were available and teachable: they left possessions, relationships and businesses to follow Jesus without excuses, and they listened eagerly and asked him to explain. Believers are urged to distinguish immaturity from lack of commitment and to yield themselves fully to Christ.
30130:
Opening the detailed studies in the series on the twelve apostles, this sermon looks at Andrew, the quiet fisherman usually known simply as Simon Peter's brother. He wrote no book, preached no recorded sermon and performed no recorded miracle, yet Christ used him mightily. His life shows what it means to be teachable and available. He was teachable because he hungered for the Word: he travelled long distances to hear John the Baptist's uncompromising preaching rather than settle for comfortable teaching, pressed Jesus privately for deeper understanding, and let hard truth change him. He was available because he hungered for the God of the Word. When John declared "Behold, the Lamb of God" (John 1:35-39), Andrew immediately followed Jesus and asked where he was staying, resolved from his first day to live his life around Christ.

The result was impact, for his eyes were always scanning for souls. The first thing he did was find his brother and bring him to Jesus (John 1:41-42), and that brother became the leader of the apostles. Later he brought seeking Greeks to Christ (John 12:20-22) and pointed to a boy's small lunch before the feeding of the five thousand, trusting Christ's power rather than human resources. Believers are urged to be faithful signposts to Jesus, serving gladly out of the spotlight with whatever little they have.
30131:
Continuing the series on the twelve apostles, this sermon looks at Philip, a cautious, detailed, by-the-book man whose security rested in his own intellect rather than in Christ. Philip is not the hero of the story but a window onto the patience and sufficiency of the Saviour, seen at three points in his life. In John 1:43-45 Jesus finds Philip and calls him to follow, and Philip tells Nathanael that he has found the Messiah. Yet salvation always begins with God: no one seeks him unless the Father draws them (Romans 3; John 6:44), so believers should be deeply grateful and the unconverted should cry out to Christ now. In John 6, Jesus tests Philip before feeding the five thousand. Philip runs the numbers and concludes it is impossible, overlooking the all-powerful Lord standing beside him.

In John 14:8-10, after three years with Jesus, Philip asks to be shown the Father, as though Christ were not enough. Jesus patiently answers that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. Philip had studied the signposts without beholding the one they pointed to. Christians are warned that they can know much about Jesus yet think too little of him, and that ministry at church or at home without his strength is death. Ordinary people who stay teachable and available can be mightily used by Christ.
30132:
Preached for weary saints facing pressures and trials, this sermon on John 21:1-14, "Breakfast on the Beach", shows the risen Christ revealing himself to his disciples in two comforting ways. First, he is our provision. Seven disciples, Peter among them still carrying his denial, have returned to Galilee in obedience to Jesus' command, yet they fish all night and catch nothing. Obedience does not remove hardship, but Jesus stands on the shore watching over them and calls them "children", his little ones. At his word the net fills with 153 large fish. Without him there is emptiness; with him there is satisfaction. As Creator he provides every meal and every breath, and even trials are part of his providence, weaning his people from the world. Peter throws himself into the sea, wanting Jesus more than the fish.

Second, Jesus is our compassion. He has already prepared a charcoal fire with fish and bread, and he serves the weary men breakfast with his own hands, just as he once washed their feet. The sermon closes with a long reading of New Testament commands, the obedience God blesses as a way of living once saved, in the Spirit's power. Christians are urged to long for Jesus more than his gifts and to keep going even when the net is empty.
30133:
Continuing the series on the twelve apostles, this sermon studies Nathanael, also called Bartholomew, from John 1:43-51. The whole series rests on one encouragement: if Christ chose and changed such ordinary, flawed men, he can use anyone who is available and teachable. When Philip announces that he has found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Nathanael scoffs, "Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?" He let outward appearances shape his view of Christ, missing that the Messiah's humble origins were part of his greatness, the same humility that led him to the cross. Believers are warned not to let trials, sickness or unanswered prayer build a wall that hides the greatness of Christ.

Philip simply says, "Come and see", and Jesus greets Nathanael as an Israelite in whom there is no deceit: not a sinless man, but one who did not hide or excuse his sin as the self-righteous leaders did. Jesus' knowledge of him under the fig tree shows that Christ knows every secret of the heart, and the sermon draws comfort from this, since he knows his people's worst and still loves them. Nathanael confesses him as Rabbi, Son of God and King of Israel, and Jesus promises he will see greater things. With Paul in Philippians 3, listeners are urged to press on to know Christ.
30134:
Continuing the series on the twelve apostles, this sermon turns to two of the least known, James the son of Alphaeus and Thaddeus. The Twelve appear in three groups of four, and these men belong to the last, the group the Gospels say least about. Their names do them no favours: Thaddeus can be read as "mama's boy" and James is called "the less", the little or least important one. Yet they were teachable and available, and when Peter said "we have left everything and followed you" in Mark 10, they stood among those for whom Christ was worth more than anything they had left behind. They represent the unknown army of the Lord: the prayer warriors, the faithful servants and the quiet workers through whom the church actually grows.

Mark 10:35-45 then shows what greatness means in God's kingdom. James and John sought the top positions, but Jesus taught that greatness is found not in rank, gifts or fame but in becoming a servant, even a slave, of all the brethren, following the Son of Man who came to serve and give his life as a ransom for many. Believers are urged to pray "use me" and let the Lord choose how, to serve without seeking applause, and to keep returning to Christ for strength so they do not burn out.
30136:
Opening a study of 1 Peter 3:18-22, often called one of the hardest passages in the Bible, this sermon focuses on verse 18 alone: Christ died for sins once for all, the just for the unjust, to bring us to God. Peter is writing to a persecuted church, and he reminds them that Christ also suffered. Jesus was no murderer, thief or blasphemer, yet he bore the wrath of God in his own body, so no believer's suffering will ever compare with his. Every death is deserved because all have sinned, but his alone was unjust, planned by God and purposeful. Because he offered himself once for all, his sacrifice covers past, present and future sins, and salvation is Christ alone, not Christ plus church attendance, Bible reading or good works.

The just died for the unjust, and Scripture's record of Moses, Paul, Rahab, David, the thief on the cross and Peter shows that no sinner is beyond his reach. He does more than make salvation available: he personally brings his people to God. Believers are called to remember that suffering for God's glory is never wasted, to stop deciding who might be saved, and to love the unlovable and keep proclaiming the gospel. The unconverted are urged to come to Christ for rest now.
30137:
Continuing in 1 Peter 3, this sermon works through one of the most debated passages in the New Testament, verses 19 to 22, to show that Christ is victorious over every power. Peter wrote to believers under persecution, and behind that hostility stands an enemy who has opposed God since the fall. Weighing several interpretations, the sermon concludes that after his death Christ went and proclaimed his triumph, not a second chance of salvation, to imprisoned fallen angels who sinned in the days of Noah, linking the passage with Genesis 6, 2 Peter 2 and Jude. Their rebellion and the corruption of that age resemble the sexual sin and spiritual darkness of our own culture.

God showed great patience while Noah preached and built the ark, yet only eight people were saved. Peter presents Christ as the better ark: he bore the judgment, carries his people through it and, raised and ascended, now reigns with angels and powers subject to him. Believers are encouraged that Satan can do nothing beyond God's permission, and that they should keep proclaiming the gospel patiently even when few respond and many mock. The sermon closes with an urgent appeal to come to Christ now, because God's patience will not wait forever and the door of the ark will one day be shut.
30139:
Thomas has long carried the label "doubting Thomas," but this sermon argues that doubt was not his defining trait, since all the disciples struggled to believe in the resurrection. What stands out in the Gospel of John is a pessimistic temperament. When Jesus resolved to return to Judea to raise Lazarus, Thomas expected only death, and on the night before the cross he answered the promise of a prepared place with "we do not know the way." Negativity drains joy, breeds self-preservation and gives Christ the bare minimum. The remedy is not mere positive thinking but filling the mind with what is excellent and praiseworthy, above all Christ himself.

Yet Thomas also showed real courage. Bravery is not the absence of fear but following Christ when every part of you is afraid, as Jesus did in Gethsemane, and Thomas urged the others to go and die with their Master. Grieving deeply after the crucifixion, he refused to believe the reports of the resurrection. Jesus came to him with peace, offered his wounds and called him to believe. Thomas responded with the highest confession in the Gospels, "My Lord and my God." Because Christ is risen, the payment for sin is accepted, death is defeated and believers will rise to enjoy him forever.
30143:
Continuing the series on the twelve apostles, this sermon traces how the grace of God transformed John, the young fisherman Jesus named a Son of Thunder. John was likely a teenager when he began following Christ, and he came from a devoted family. His mother Salome followed Jesus from Galilee to Jerusalem, supported his ministry, stood at the cross and went early to the tomb. His father Zebedee released his sons and wife to follow Christ at real cost to himself. Their example challenges parents to treasure Christ above comfort, wealth or success and to give their children Christ, and calls young people to be wholehearted for Jesus while they are young.

Yet John badly needed grace. Soon after seeing Christ's glory on the mountain he argued over who was greatest, tried to stop a man casting out demons in Jesus' name, and wanted to call fire down on a Samaritan village. Jesus patiently corrected him and then showed him love at the cross, where he forgave his enemies and entrusted his mother to John's care. That grace remade John into the apostle of love, who later preached to the Samaritans and wrote that believers ought to lay down their lives for one another. The sermon calls listeners with anger, control or impatience to be teachable and available, because grace does not only forgive but continues to change.
